articles.title: Supreme Court sides with Trump administration on mail voting restrictions ahead of midterms
articles.summary: The Supreme Court opened a path Monday for possible implementation of President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, though it remains...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court opened a path Monday for possible implementation of President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, though it remains unclear how much can be put in place before the fast-approaching midterm elections.

The decision leaves room for additional court challenges that could further slow Trump's order, and other similar cases have already been filed. The U.S. Postal Service laid out how it would implement the order last week, but time is running short to impose major changes. North Carolina is sending out ballots Sept. 4 overseas and to military voters, and other states will quickly follow suit in just a few weeks.

The Supreme Court's conservative majority didn't decide the legality of Trump's order, instead ruling that states who sued did not have the legal right to challenge it.

While the emergency order is not final, it does have the potential to create chaos around voting across the country, with Trump often questioning the integrity of elections and the nation's highest court again the possible arbiter of a political controversy.

"The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell," the majority wrote in an unsigned order.

The three liberal-leaning justices publicly dissented, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson writing that the rule "lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges."

New York Attorney General Letitia James foreshadowed more legal fights ahead, calling the decision a "painful setback" but vowing it would "not be the final word."

The court's order opens a path for the administration to begin action to restrict mail voting, but it also could lead to further litigation that could freeze the federal government again.

"This is just the first inning of a very fast nine-inning game," said Derek Muller, a law professor at Notre Dame University.

Democrat-led states push back against Trump's order

Mail balloting has long been a favorite target for Trump, who has claimed that it breeds fraud despite strong evidence to the contrary and his own use of the voting method .

Trump's executive order, signed in March, calls on his administration to create lists of eligible voters and orders the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists. New requirements released Friday would forbid the Postal Service from sending mail ballots from any state that does not comply with Trump's order.

A Postal Service spokesperson did not immediately respond messages seeking comment. The White House did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.

Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued to block the order. They argued that the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to run elections, and Trump's changes could lead to chaos and partisan abuse.

"The consequences of allowing such transformative changes to take effect so close to this fall's elections would be extreme," attorneys for the states wrote. Dozens of state and local election officials weighed in, asking the justices to leave the order frozen while election preparations are already underway.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said Monday the order was aimed at making it "harder for Americans to vote" in the pivotal elections for control of Congress, and vowed that Democrats would "fight every attempt to hijack mail-in voting and rig the rules before voters have their say this November."

A judge in Massachusetts blocked the plan for the midterm elections in those states. An appeals court upheld her decision. She later granted a second order blocking it nationwide in a separate case, another remaining stumbling block for the Trump administration, which Monday night asked her to void or suspend it in light of the Supreme Court ruling.

The Justice Department appealed to the Supreme Court on procedural grounds in late July, arguing that the states sued too soon. They also pointed to another ruling out of Washington, where a judge allowed Trump's order to proceed. An appeals court backed that decision, while still leaving room for future court action if the changes are implemented.

Federal attorneys argued that the Massachusetts order "blocks the government's ability to finalize and implement the President's proposed policies to promote election integrity for the upcoming federal elections in November."

A dozen Republican-leaning states supported the federal government in their own appeal before the high court, saying states would have input on the final voter lists.

Trump fights mail-in voting despite its growing popularity

The Supreme Court has previously ruled against Trump-backed arguments on mail-in ballots, finding in a 5-4 decision that states can count ballots that arrive after Election Day. That case was decided after full briefing and arguments, rather than on the court's emergency docket.

Trump has blamed mail voting — without credible evidence — for his loss to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. He has promoted the proposed changes in his executive order as safeguards to keep non-U.S. citizens from voting.

He's also repeatedly pressed for the passage of the legislation that requires proof of citizenship to vote. Noncitizen voting has been shown to be exceedingly rare, and is a felony that can be punishable by deportation.

Using mail ballots has become increasingly popular with voters of both parties, with about 30% of all ballots cast that way during the 2024 presidential election, according to federal data. The process also is secure. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found only about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million mail ballots cast.

David Becker, a former justice department lawyer who co-wrote a book debunking Trump's 2020 election lies, said the high court created "pure chaos leading up to the midterm elections, waiting weeks after an administration filing, and just days before mail ballots go out, to completely rewrite the rules."

Riccardi reported from Denver. Associated Press writer John Hanna in Topeka, Kansas contributed to this report.

articles.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
articles.summary: Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands and West Yorkshire as well as Â£6bn for London.
articles.body:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost Â£10bn in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional Â£6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes, under the government's Â£39bn social housebuilding programme.

Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".

Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire Â£39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

Under Labour, homeless figures have continued to rise to record levels and data released earlier this month suggested 177,530 children were homeless in temporary accommodation.

Natasha, who has been living in a hotel in Milton Keynes for the last four months with her son Zayd, is one of those waiting for a permanent home.

The 22-year-old spent the final months of her pregnancy and the first weeks of her son's life living in a hotel.

She told BBC's Your Voice she has no idea how long she will be expected to stay there but was told it would only be temporary.

"I'm just scared when he gets older, when he starts crawling around, I can't even allow him to crawl in such a place like that because it's so dirty," she says.

While pregnant, Natasha says her room became infested with ants, which she repeatedly reported before eventually being moved into another room.

While Natasha has her own bathroom, she shares a kitchen with around 60 other residents. She says the hotel is home to a mix of people, not just mothers and babies, and that she does not always feel safe using the shared space with Zayd.

Natasha describes living there as feeling "like a prison". She says visitors are not allowed, meaning friends and family can not come to help her with her five-week-old boy.

She is one of the 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

London will see the largest share of funding, although no figure has been given for how many homes will be built in the capital.

Ministers said Monday's allocation was the first stage of the 10-year programme and more than Â£16bn remains to be allocated outside London.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested some of the new homes will be built by councils, saying she and the prime minister were "doing everything we can to get councils building once again".

Speaking on a visit to a housing development in south-east London, she told the BBC she understood the "frustration of people who are in temporary accommodation at the moment or on one of those waiting lists".

But she insisted that she and the prime minister "are doing everything we can to get councils building once again".

Burnham had previously promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period", but the announcement stops short of clarifying how the funding will be split between council homes and those provided by housing associations.

In the 1950s, councils were building almost 200,000 new council homes a year, but half of councils do not currently own or build their own homes.

In 2024 to 2025, around 65,000 new affordable homes were completed in England. Of those, there were just over 12,000 built for social rent - the highest since 2013 to 2014.

Organisations such as the National Housing Federation and homeless charities have previously agreed that at least 90,000 social homes would need to be built each year to meet demand.

Charlie Berry, policy manager at housing charity Shelter, said the announcement was "not near the level we need to truly tackle that backlog and end homelessness".

But she said it was a "significant improvement", and added she would "love" Rayner to commit to a target of how many socially rented homes will be built annually.

Conservative shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly described the announcement as "sleight of hand", saying: "The small print shows homes won't have to be delivered until 2039."

He said: "Fewer homes will be delivered than previous programmes in this Parliament as social rent is more expensive. Labour have scaled back their affordable housing programme and expect us to thank them for it."

The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election which they estimated would "free up" 228,144 homes for "British families".

On Monday, Reform UK announced similar plans to prioritise British-born workers under 35 when allocating social housing if it were to enter government.

Liberal Democrat housing spokesperson Gideon Amos welcomed parts of the government's plan, but said the plan for more social rent homes "won't cut it" and a programme is needed that "meets the scale of the challenge".

As well as the promise and funding to build more social homes, the Labour government pledged to build 1.5 million homes by 2029.

So far Labour is not on track to meet that target.

BBC Verify has been tracking the target using government statistics on the number of Energy Performance Certificates (EPC) issued by each local authority. Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built.

The latest EPC data suggests about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England in the 12 months ending June 2026. To reach the government's target of 1.5 million homes over five years, there would need to be at least 300,000.

articles.title: Ronaldo Caiado pede ao STF abertura de sigilo sobre INSS e Master | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PSD à Presidência afirma que medida evitaria que eleitores fossem “enganados” por eventuais candidatos envolvidos em crimes. Os jornalistas Renata Vasconcellos e César Tralli conduzem nesta semana entrevistas da Globo com os presidenciáveis.
articles.summary: Ronaldo Caiado solicita ao STF a abertura de sigilos sobre fraudes no INSS e propõe anistia aos condenados pelo 8 de janeiro em entrevista sobre suas propostas.
articles.body:
O candidato do PSD à Presidência, Ronaldo Caiado, encerrou entrevista nesta terça-feira (25) à Globo fazendo um apelo ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) para que sejam abertos sigilos relacionados ao INSS, ao caso Master e à Operação Carbono Oculto.

Segundo ele, a medida permitiria que os eleitores tivessem conhecimento de eventuais crimes envolvendo candidatos antes da eleição.

“Eu pediria que eles refletissem bem e abrissem o sigilo do INSS, do caso Master, e juntassem a ele também toda essa parte do Carbono Oculto, para que nós não fôssemos amanhã enganados [por] pessoas envolvidas em graves crimes e que amanhã pudessem ser eleitas”, afirmou.

As investigações citadas por Caiado desgastam os candidatos Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT).

Ao longo da entrevista, Caiado também apresentou propostas para a segurança pública e a economia . O candidato defendeu a criação de uma polícia transnacional entre países da América Latina, com troca de informações de inteligência e possibilidade de realizar prisões nos países participantes. Segundo ele, o avanço do narcotráfico transformou o Brasil no “maior hub” da atividade na região e representa uma ameaça inclusive às exportações brasileiras.

Na área econômica, o candidato do PSD prometeu propor um ajuste fiscal por meio de uma emenda à Constituição, limitando o crescimento das despesas do governo federal à inflação mais 50% do crescimento do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB).

Questionado sobre os cálculos que embasam a proposta, pediu “calma” e comparou a situação das contas públicas à de um paciente atropelado que ainda precisa ser examinado.

O candidato também reafirmou que, se eleito, concederá anistia aos condenados pela tentativa de golpe de Estado de 8 de Janeiro, incluindo o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

Caiado voltou a comparar a discussão à soltura do presidente Lula (PT) e à recuperação dos direitos políticos do petista, em 2021, após as condenações na Lava Jato.

Confira as datas das entrevistas com candidatos a presidente para a Globo

A entrevista com Caiado foi a segunda de uma série com os candidatos à Presidência da República. A Globo convidou os seis candidatos mais bem posicionados na pesquisa de intenção de voto divulgada pela Quaest em 14 de agosto. A ordem das entrevistas foi definida por sorteio, com a presença de representantes dos partidos.

24 de agosto (segunda-feira): Romeu Zema (Novo)

25 de agosto (terça-feira): Ronaldo Caiado (PSD)

26 de agosto (quarta-feira): Renan Santos (Missão)

27 de agosto (quinta-feira): Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT)

28 de agosto (sexta-feira): Flávio Bolsonaro (PL)

29 de agosto (sábado): Augusto Cury (Avante)

Esta é a primeira vez que as entrevistas da Globo com candidatos ao Palácio do Planalto são após o Jornal Nacional, e não dentro do telejornal. Após a exibição, a entrevista vai ficar disponível na íntegra no g1 e no Globoplay.

O 1º turno das eleições será em 4 de outubro.

articles.title: Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. Will that change in November?
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton, a liberal megachurch pastor, is challenging incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall in this year’s midterm election
articles.body:
In one of the first ads of his campaign to represent Kansas in the US Senate, the Democrat Adam Hamilton stands grilling steaks at a barbecue and attacks his opponent, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, for supporting "tariffs and war".

If history is any guide, it is Hamilton who is set to get cooked. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close. But he and his supporters believe circumstances have conspired to end this streak – and potentially deliver Democrats control of the Senate.

"When it comes to tariffs, healthcare, immigration, when it comes to the war in Iran, these are all things that are having a negative impact on people in Kansas," Hamilton, 62, said in an interview. "That makes this a particularly vulnerable time for Roger Marshall. Then, I think I'm a particularly strong candidate. I wouldn't have got in the race if I didn't."

The founder of the largest Methodist denomination in the US, Hamilton won 35% of the vote in the 11-candidate Democratic primary earlier this month. His campaign recently announced he had broken a quarterly fundraising record in the state, and two major election forecasters say the Senate race has grown more competitive since Hamilton won his party's primary, though Marshall is still favored to win.

For national Democratic leaders, the possibility of a close Senate race in Kansas is enticing. Their path to retaking Congress's upper chamber involves winning at least three seats in states that Donald Trump carried two years ago, and they've named Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Iowa as among their best bets to do so.

The US president's slumping approval ratings and the Iran war's impact on prices for gasoline and other staples are seen as boosting Democrats' chances in those states, but Kansas is a bit redder. Trump carried it two years ago by a 16 percentage point margin.

This week, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer told Punchbowl News that if the November elections wind up producing a "blue wave" of Democratic victories, Hamilton may well win.

Asked what he thought of Schumer's prediction, Hamilton said: "I don't agree with that. I think there will be a blue wave, but I'm telling you, here in Kansas, we have a real chance to win. I don't care what else happens across the country."

No Kansas Democrat has won a full term in the US Senate since attorney George McGill in 1932, the longest streak of any state. In 1974, Senator Bob Dole, who would go on to become the chamber's Republican leader and run unsuccessfully against President Bill Clinton in 1996, nearly lost his bid for a second term, but Republicans have wiped out their opponents ever since.

Democrats and their causes have had better luck at the state level. The governor's mansion has seesawed between the two parties since the late 1950s, and the race this year to replace outgoing Democratic governor Laura Kelly is viewed as a toss-up. After the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade, Kansans have on two occasions rejected Republican-backed attempts to curb abortion access in the state.

"Kansas voters, the majority anyway, there's something about the Senate where, especially those moderate Republicans, still won't pull the trigger in terms of enough of them voting for a Democrat, where they will for governor," said Bob Beatty, a longtime state politics watcher who chairs the political science department at Washburn University in Topeka.

But Hamilton's experience in leading a church gives him a unique skill set that Beatty predicts will make for "a very competitive race" against Marshall. "What Hamilton has going for him is the communication side. He's been giving sermons, AKA speeches, to crowds of thousands for years," he said.

Marshall is an OB/GYN who represented western Kansas in the US House of Representatives, then won election to the Senate in 2020 and embraced Trump's debunked claims of fraud in that year's presidential vote. He has been an ally of Trump in Congress, and last year left a town hall early after attendees pressed him about the Trump administration's funding cuts and layoffs of federal employees. A spokesperson for the senator did not respond to a request for comment.

Hamilton said he decided to jump into the Senate race ahead of Easter, as he prepared to preach the sermon on the mount at his Church of the Resurrection outside Kansas City, which boasts around 24,000 congregants. He mulled running as an independent, but ultimately filed as a Democrat, saying he was concerned that he'd split the vote if he wasn't in a party and agreed with its views on "healthcare, education [and] social safety nets".

"Those are things that matter a lot to me, and my faith leads in that direction," he said.

A self-described "moderate or independent-minded Democrat", his campaign recently released an ad where Hamilton likens Kansas's position in the middle of the country to his own approach to the politics that would await him in Washington DC.

Hamilton has criticized Marshall for being "a spokesperson for Washington and Donald Trump instead of representing the people of Kansas", and accused the senator of spending most of his time in Florida. Marshall has acknowledged owning a property in that state, but recently told reporters it was destroyed by a hurricane. Earlier this month, the Topeka Capital-Journal reported he'd put the Sarasota property on the market for $1.45m.

The senator recently called his opponent a "megachurch pastor that's too woke for Kansas", the Capital-Journal reported. Main Street Fund, a Massachusetts-based Super Pac that lists its treasurer a consultant who has worked for Republican campaigns, spent more than $600,000 this month to air ads in Kansas, making a similar accusation against Hamilton that the Kansas City Star found relied on snippets from his sermons that were taken out of context.

Like so much in his career, Hamilton's chances may come down to faith. Jim Slattery, a Democratic former congressman from the state who supports Hamilton, described him as "a known quantity in the Methodist world in Kansas" and among Christians in the Kansas City area who may win if he gains the support of right-leaning Catholic voters opposed to the war with Iran.

"The reason Hamilton is a compelling candidate is because he can, and he has the ability to, dramatically expand the audience for a Democrat candidate in Kansas," Slattery said. "It's the bottom line."

articles.title: Poll: Republicans' chances of controlling Congress in 2027 appear shaky
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Four months out from the 2026 midterm elections, Republicans’ chances of maintaining control of Congress appear slim, new polling shows...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Four months out from the 2026 midterm elections, Republicans' chances of maintaining control of Congress appear slim, new polling shows.

The Center Square's newest Voters' Voice Poll revealed that 47% of U.S. registered voters surveyed would vote for a Democratic candidate if elections were held today, while 42% would vote for a Republican. Nine percent of voters haven't made up their minds yet.

The poll was conducted by Noble Predictive Insights from Aug. 12-16, surveying 2,533 registered U.S. voters. The sample was comprised of 930 Republicans, 930 Democrats, and 673 Independents. Among independent voters, 330 respondents were classified as True Independents, or individuals who do not lean toward either major party when given the choice. The poll's margin of error is +/- 2.0%.

While the leanings of members in either of the two major political parties remain relatively stable, swing voters' choices pose a growing threat to Republicans' control of both chambers, as they do today with slim margins in both the U.S. House and Senate. Only 33% of Independents total chose a Republican candidate, while 40% chose a Democratic candidate and 20% are still unsure.

Although more than half of True Independents remain undecided, those who have decided are veering to the Democrats, with 20% choosing the Democratic candidate versusl 10% choosing the Republican.

Critical bipartisan legislation funding farmers and road infrastructure has lagged in Congress, and Republicans in both chambers initially blocked War Powers Resolutions to halt military hostilities in Iran that are driving up gas and food prices.

Notably, groups particularly sensitive to the rising costs of living are turning to Democrats, who have criticized recent price increases due to the Iran conflict, President Donald Trump's tariff policies, and Republican infighting or inaction in Congress over cost-of-living issues like healthcare and housing.

The median annual household income in the U.S. was $83,730 in 2024, according to the United States Census Bureau.

The August Voters' Voice Poll showed that Americans earning under $50,000 per year favored Democrats over Republicans, 50% to 37%.

The median income for Black households was about $32,000 less than that, while the median income for Hispanic voters was approximately $18,000 less than the overall median income. Over two-thirds of Black voters and 59% of Hispanic voters chose a Democratic candidate in the poll.

Younger voters ages 18-29, who typically have the lowest salaries of any nonretired age group, also leaned left, with 54% supporting a Democrat and 36% supporting a Republican. Just one of the four age groups polled favored Republicans — 30 to 44-year-olds, 51% of them.

Mike Noble, founder and CEO of Noble Predictive Insights, told The Center Square that the generational differences displayed in the poll most likely reflect each group's economic concerns.

"You see that younger voters, especially 18 through 29, who Trump definitely made inroads with last time, they've really fallen away. Economically, they've been hit the hardest," Noble said. "And then 30 to 44, they usually get a little better income earnings at that point, they're doing decently better. They prefer the Republican candidate – they're kind of the populous crowd that [President Donald] Trump really dug into from the beginning."

Female voters, whose median income in 2024 was about $14,000 less than males', supported a Democratic candidate by 52% and a Republican candidate by 35% in the poll, with 11% remaining unsure.

By contrast, 51% male voters surveyed supported Republicans, while 40% supported Democrats and 7% remained unsure.

Even without Republicans' political woes, political parties in power generally perform poorly during midterm elections.

"The main takeaway in the environment right now is that the Democrats really have that edge, and the race is still a little bit fluid with the True Independents," Noble said. "People care more about these economic issues right now, and that's where the pain point is."

articles.title: Harvard Professor Warns That AI Execs Are Pushing World Toward Factory Farming of Humans
articles.summary: "Who decided this is a way we should be living?"
articles.body:
We're racing towards a future where AI enables the "factory farming of humans," a Harvard professor warns — if tech elites get their way, at least.

In a new episode of The New York Time's "Hard Fork" podcast, the historian Jill Lepore discusses her idea of an "artificial state" that's supplanting the traditional nation state, and particular constitutional democracy, with one that erases human autonomy.

In this emerging world order, government is conducted "not by the consent of people but by machines that are making decisions," she explained on the podcast. And those machines, of course, are owned by corporations.

We aren't living in the artificial state quite yet, Lepore stresses, but it's something that's being built and realized around us. And crucially, it's also a fantasy held by certain influential elites who believe their power should supersede the actual government and the voters who decide how it's run.

"The rhetoric that comes out of this particular historical moment is really about the evanescence of modern liberal democracy, constitutional democracy," she said. The elites pushing this rhetoric aren't "interested in what the people want," she added. "Because actually, what the people want is not to have AI and not to have data centers. So that's the crisis."

Lepore explores the idea in depth in her upcoming book " The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State ." She was inspired by a simple question: in our current world where you're forced to talk to an AI to get answers, ranging from when you call in to ask about an appointment or talk to a company's support chatbot on its website, "who decided this is a way we should be living?"

The artificial state is a sort of backsliding, in which more and more of the state's functions are now being replaced by corporations that own and control our digital communications infrastructure. How we get our news, and information on elections and who to vote for, is all being mediated by these powerful groups — through technologies like the TV and radio, once, and now social media being the increasingly dominant medium.

The digital communication our lives are now structured around have a powerful isolating effect. In her 2024 piece for The New Yorker where she initially explored the idea that would later become her book, Lepore described the artificial state as the "factory farming of public life, the sorting and segmenting, the isolation and alienation, the destruction of human community."

The artificial state isn't purely driven by AI, but it's certainly being accelerated by it. People are asking ChatGPT about who to vote for , rather than talking to their neighbors, local officials, or experts. The political messages they're seeing, meanwhile, are probably in part being written with AI . Decisions at every level are being made with the assistance of thinking machines . AI is also entrenching surveillance , processing the mountains of data that is being gathered on all of us.

One nefarious aspect of the pro-AI rhetoric coming out of Silicon Valley is that it frames AI as an inevitability. But Lepore argued that this brand of fatalism is a "bogus premise," itself nestled on top of several more dubious propositions. One we hear endlessly is that regulation stifles innovation, so the government should take the handbrake off AI development. The other is that technology always advances democracy, which assures us that all of the very real threats to democracy AI poses in the present will magically sort themselves out.

Neither of those are true, Lepore says, and you have to look no further than how similar promises were made for technologies in the recent past.

"So now, the AI people come back with the same argument that was made about the internet — the personal computer, the internet, and social media," she said in the interview.

More on AI: Trump Says You're a Rube If You Don't Want a Data Center in Your Backyard

articles.title: Pirro hit with bar complaint over bid to indict Democrats in illegal orders video
articles.summary: A legal watchdog has filed a bar complaint against U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, arguing she violated various standards in seeking to bring charges against six Democratic lawmakers who filmed a video noting that military members can refuse illegal orders. The complaint from the Legal Accountability Center asks the New York…
articles.body:
A legal watchdog has filed a bar complaint against U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, arguing she violated various standards in seeking to bring charges against six Democratic lawmakers who filmed a video noting that military members can refuse illegal orders.

The complaint from the Legal Accountability Center asks the New York court system’s Grievance Committee to investigate Pirro, saying she violated rules of professional conduct.

A grand jury ultimately declined to bring charges related to the video, which shows the six lawmakers, each with military and intelligence backgrounds, speaking directly to active service members and saying, “Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders.”

But the filing from the center argues Pirro’s directive to prosecutors to bring the case was “unwarranted, frivolous, and would serve merely to harass or maliciously injure the targets of her order” and that “she knew or should have known, as a government prosecutor, that her directive to seek indictments was not legally or factually supported by ‘probable cause.’”

“By directing the said AUSAs to seek meritless indictments against the Trump administration’s perceived political enemies, she thereby engaged in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice,” the group wrote in the filing , using an abbreviation for assistant U.S. attorneys.

The video outraged President Trump, who called it “SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!”

Prosecutors planned to charge the six lawmakers under a law that forbids “interference with the loyalty, morale or discipline of the U.S. Armed Forces,” though a grand jury found prosecutors did not bring sufficient evidence to justify bringing changes.

Tim Lauer, a spokesperson for Pirro, called the complaint frivolous.

“The grand jury, not the prosecutor, decides whether to indict. That is their job. Attempting to weaponize the disciplinary process against prosecutors for doing their jobs amounts to nothing more than a frivolous complaint,” he said in a statement.

Additional complaints were filed against the two prosecutors who brought the case at Pirro’s direction, made in New York and Virginia.

The Legal Accountability Center said the video was clearly protected speech and that it should have been apparent to prosecutors they had no case.

“Regarding the requirement of ‘probable cause,’ it should be evident that Ms. Pirro knew or should have known that none existed. How could it, when the comments at issue were plainly protected First Amendment speech,” they wrote.

Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), one of the six lawmakers in the video, said he counted Pirro as one of Trump’s “stooges” for bringing “bogus criminal charges” against him and the others.

“They have weaponized our Justice Department, attempting to silence dissent and anyone who stands up to their lawlessness. Their efforts will not succeed because the American people are fed up with their corruption and failed policies. Accountability is coming,” he said in a statement.
paragraphs: A legal watchdog has filed a bar complaint against U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, arguing she violated various standards in seeking to bring charges against six Democratic lawmakers who filmed a video noting that military members can refuse illegal orders.
The complaint from the Legal Accountability Center asks the New York court system’s Grievance Committee to investigate Pirro, saying she violated rules of professional conduct.

A grand jury ultimately declined to bring charges related to the video, which shows the six lawmakers, each with military and intelligence backgrounds, speaking directly to active service members and saying, “Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders.”

But the filing from the center argues Pirro’s directive to prosecutors to bring the case was “unwarranted, frivolous, and would serve merely to harass or maliciously injure the targets of her order” and that “she knew or should have known, as a government prosecutor, that her directive to seek indictments was not legally or factually supported by ‘probable cause.’”

“By directing the said AUSAs to seek meritless indictments against the Trump administration’s perceived political enemies, she thereby engaged in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice,” the group wrote in the filing , using an abbreviation for assistant U.S. attorneys.
The video outraged President Trump, who called it “SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!”

Prosecutors planned to charge the six lawmakers under a law that forbids “interference with the loyalty, morale or discipline of the U.S. Armed Forces,” though a grand jury found prosecutors did not bring sufficient evidence to justify bringing changes.
Tim Lauer, a spokesperson for Pirro, called the complaint frivolous.

“The grand jury, not the prosecutor, decides whether to indict. That is their job. Attempting to weaponize the disciplinary process against prosecutors for doing their jobs amounts to nothing more than a frivolous complaint,” he said in a statement.
Additional complaints were filed against the two prosecutors who brought the case at Pirro’s direction, made in New York and Virginia.
The Legal Accountability Center said the video was clearly protected speech and that it should have been apparent to prosecutors they had no case.

“Regarding the requirement of ‘probable cause,’ it should be evident that Ms. Pirro knew or should have known that none existed. How could it, when the comments at issue were plainly protected First Amendment speech,” they wrote.
Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), one of the six lawmakers in the video, said he counted Pirro as one of Trump’s “stooges” for bringing “bogus criminal charges” against him and the others.

“They have weaponized our Justice Department, attempting to silence dissent and anyone who stands up to their lawlessness. Their efforts will not succeed because the American people are fed up with their corruption and failed policies. Accountability is coming,” he said in a statement.

articles.title: Lawmakers across the aisle pay tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘A true national treasure’
articles.summary: The death of Dolly Parton is uniting lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, with an outpouring from Democrats and Republicans alike mourning the loss of the “true national treasure.” The country music singer and songwriter died at 80 in Nashville, Tenn., Tuesday. “Dolly Parton was loved in every corner of our nation,” Senate Minority Leader…
articles.body:
The death of Dolly Parton is uniting lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, with an outpouring from Democrats and Republicans alike mourning the loss of the “true national treasure.”

The country music singer and songwriter died at 80 in Nashville, Tenn., Tuesday.

“Dolly Parton was loved in every corner of our nation,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a social platform X post shortly after news of the music legend’s death broke.

“All of America is mourning this monumental loss. We love you, Dolly,” Schumer said, calling the Imagination Library founder a “force for good.”

“America has lost a true national treasure,” Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said.

“Parton’s unmistakable voice, joyful spirit, and remarkable generosity touched generations of Americans and many others around the world. From the mountains of Tennessee to stages across the globe, she never forgot where she came from, and she used her extraordinary success to lift up countless others,” Johnson said.

Parton, Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) said, was “Americana personified!”

“World famous and self-deprecating at the same time. We will never see another like her. What a life, what an example!” Wicker said .

Rep. Steve Cohen (D-Tenn.) called the Volunteer State-born entertainer the “ greatest representative of Tennessee ever.”

“Not just from her musical talents and her philanthropy, but from her big heart and amazing grace. She made us all proud,” Cohen said.

“Rest in Peace, Dolly — you were truly an American Icon,” Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) wrote on social media . “You will be dearly missed.”

“I join every American in mourning the incredibly sad news that Dolly Parton has passed away,” Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) said.

“Dolly was a music icon who inspired so many people and always gave back to her community, from supporting children’s literacy through her Imagination Library to helping end the COVID pandemic through her donation for vaccine research,” Rosen said .

Parton, the House Republican conference said on X , “was an American icon. A legendary artist, a generous philanthropist, and a proud daughter of Tennessee whose music and spirit touched generations of Americans.”

“This is devastating news,” Rep. Rebecca Balint (D-Vt.) said.

“Yes, Dolly was an legendary songwriter, but she was also a ray of sunshine for all and a true community servant that brought people together from all walks of life,” Balint said .

“Today, Tennessee lost one of our greatest ambassadors in Dolly Parton,” Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) said.

“Her music inspired generations of Americans, and her philanthropic work helped provide greater access to education for countless young Tennesseans,” the congressman said.

“She represented the very best of the American Dream,” Burchett said , “and her legacy will live on for generations to come.”

articles.title: Paramount’s Warner Bros. bid barrels toward antitrust trial: What to know
articles.summary: Paramount Skydance’s bid to acquire fellow entertainment giant Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) has been mired in controversy and drew a lawsuit from critics who argue the deal is bad for the movie-making and media business. As David Ellison, the company’s top executive and an ally of President Trump, wages a public relations and legal defense campaign advocating…
articles.body:
Paramount Skydance’s bid to acquire fellow entertainment giant Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) has been mired in controversy and drew a lawsuit from critics who argue the deal is bad for the movie-making and media business.

As David Ellison, the company’s top executive and an ally of President Trump, wages a public relations and legal defense campaign advocating for the merger, a Democratic-led suit seeking to stop it appears likely headed for a jury trial in California next spring.

The case took a dramatic turn this week, when California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) called off a planned settlement meeting over what he said were leaks orchestrated by Paramount publicizing details of previous meetings between the two sides, tainting the negotiating process.

The company and state government have been trading barbs in court and in the media for weeks, with Paramount’s top legal officer saying earlier this month the company was considering leaving its headquarters in Southern California if Bonta does not drop his lawsuit.

Here’s what to know about the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger saga and how it got to this point.

Paramount sets its eyes on unprecedented growth

Since it was purchased by Ellison’s Skydance Media, Paramount has undergone massive changes to its content strategy and business, aiming to acquire as many assets as it can and gearing up for a fight with major tech platforms in the streaming era.

The company is trying to fend off others like Amazon, Apple and Netflix, which are pouring hundreds of millions into the business of both scripted and unscripted entertainment, live sports and news.

Paramount’s news division, CBS, has been at the center of some of the company’s most sweeping changes, with Ellison tapping controversial journalist Bari Weiss to serve as the network’s top editor and overhauling its top news program, “60 Minutes.”

Many observers have seen Weiss’s appointment and the changes at “60 Minutes” as a rightward shift directed by Ellison to curry favor with Trump as he looks to grow his media empire.

The Warner Bros. Discovery transaction is seen by the company’s investors as crucial to that growth strategy, given WBD’s vast library of content and studios feeding both its linear and streaming channels. If the deal, announced in February and worth an estimated $110 billion, is allowed to clear, it would create the largest media company on earth and hand the Ellison family control of an unprecedented share of viewership in the United States and around the world.

Democrats, creatives raise antitrust concerns

This summer, a group of Democratic state attorneys general filed suit to stop the deal on antitrust grounds. A week later, a judge paused the acquisition , and then Paramount put the merger on hold in light of the suit.

The states, led by Bonta, argue that a combined Paramount-WBD entity would stifle competition in the media sector and ultimately negatively impact jobs and creative opportunities for actors, directors, writers and others in the entertainment industry.

“Film and television are not commodities; they are a principal means by which Americans encounter stories, ideas, and perspectives beyond their own experience,” the attorneys general wrote in their suit.

Democrats on Capitol Hill, meanwhile, are pushing back on the prospect that Ellison could gain more power in the mainstream media.

“Despite repeated promises to protect editorial independence, journalists inside CBS have described a newsroom increasingly bending to the Trump Administration’s political demands,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) wrote in a recent letter to Ellison. “Critical stories have reportedly been stalled, interviews pushed off the air, and reporters pressured to distort coverage of protests in Minneapolis and the killing of Renée Good to more closely resemble the Trump Administration’s false account.”

Raskin added CBS “pulled” a “60 Minutes” interview with Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), in which he “presented evidence that major banks facilitated Jeffrey Epstein’s illicit and illegal activities, and the reporter behind the segment was subsequently fired.”

The fear among Democrats and media watchdogs is no outlet would be more negatively impacted by the merger than Warner Bros. Discovery’s top news-gathering asset: CNN.

The cable news channel founded by the late Ted Turner has been at the center of WBD’s linear portfolio as it pitched potential buyers on acquisition.

The outlet has, however, been plagued recently by significant turnover in both its executive leadership ranks and on-air hosting roles, regularly lagging competitors in the weekly and monthly cable news viewership race.

Yet the cable channel and the future of its coverage of politics and current events remain a major point of contention around the Paramount acquisition, given Trump’s history of attacking the network and its reporters.

Trump has said he would like to see CNN operate under new ownership and praised Ellison’s efforts at CBS.

Staffers at the outlet have reportedly been unnerved by Paramount’s pursuit of the channel’s parent company, mainly with recent changes at CBS in mind.

After weeks of staying silent about the deal as criticisms grew, Ellison surprised many when he published an essay in The New York Times opinion pages defending the merger on Aug. 4. The fight, in court and in the headlines, “is not really about market share,” he wrote.

“I believe a plainer worry sits beneath the briefs and the news releases: the news. The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN,” he wrote. “There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions.”

Ellison insisted, “I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views,” and he argued the merger was necessary for legacy media companies like his to compete with Big Tech in the years to come.

“It’s the audience — the American people — who have the final say in whether a movie succeeds or fails, whether a news organization thrives or withers and therefore whether our industry succeeds or fails,” Ellison wrote in his Times op-ed. “I want to build a company with the strength and resources to deliver for those audiences who turn to us, for the storytellers who rely on us and for the country that dreamed this all up.”

Settlement talks stall as jury trial looms

Both sides in the Paramount v. California case have telegraphed a willingness to hammer out a settlement to avoid a date in court.

But those efforts have so far been fruitless.

A meeting scheduled for Monday was scrapped after Bonta accused Paramount of leaking the details of a previous meeting to media outlets, saying the company was not acting in good faith.

“As soon as Paramount stops playing games and engages sincerely, my office is happy to meet again,” Bonta said.

Paramount, which is headquartered in California and has threatened to leave the state over the lawsuit, is denying responsibility for the leaks and has said it is prepared to defend the merger in court.

“We remain hopeful and stand ready to continue good faith discussions to resolve the Attorneys General suit and move forward with our plans for increased competition and increased output to the benefit of the talent and entertainment workers,” the company said.

If no agreement between the two sides is reached, a jury trial is preliminarily slated for early March.

articles.title: Tim Scott says candidates like El-Sayed ‘coming after our culture’
articles.summary: Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) on Monday said that candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s Senate race, are “coming after our culture.” Scott told Fox News host Sean Hannity that “radical” candidates “don’t just want new policies.” “They want to change the very DNA of what it means to be American,” he continued.…
articles.body:
Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) on Monday said that candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s Senate race, are “coming after our culture.”

Scott told Fox News host Sean Hannity that “radical” candidates “don’t just want new policies.”

“They want to change the very DNA of what it means to be American,” he continued. “They’re coming for our culture, Sean, and that is what makes them dangerous.”

Scott called the upcoming November midterms “the most important midterm election in our lifetime” in a face-off between “communists and socialists against what makes America great.”

El-Sayed, a progressive, appeared on Fox News Monday night in an interview with host Jesse Watters. The two clashed as Watters asked the candidate for his opinions on topics like transgender athletes and gender-affirming care, while El-Sayed spoke more about healthcare, gas prices, the Iran war and immigration.

Twice during the interview, El-Sayed requested for Watters to “just let me answer the question.”

“Can I just tell you –– you know what you didn’t ask me about? We got a president of the United States who cares more about the drapes in a ballroom that shouldn’t be built than he cares about the war he just got us into, or that he cares about the affordability crisis,” El-Sayed said toward the end of the interview.

President Trump and many Republican lawmakers have denounced the rising tide of progressive Democrats and democratic socialists winning primary elections across the country, including in New York, Ohio and Florida.

The president has painted these candidates — including El-Sayed — as “communists” and claimed that they are a “threat” to the country .

El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) earlier this month, advancing El-Sayed to a November match-up against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), the GOP candidate.

A recent poll released by Susquehanna Polling & Research showed El-Sayed leading Rogers 46-39 among likely voters. The survey found that El-Sayed, backed by antiestablishment Democrats, holds an advantage over voters who view the economy as their most important issue.

But the poll also found that both candidates are viewed negatively by most voters, with 45 percent holding an unfavorable view of El-Sayed and 37 percent who said they view Rogers unfavorably.

articles.title: Pelosi: Trump’s effort to control mail-in voting ‘threatens to silence’ voters
articles.summary: Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) bashed a recent Supreme Court decision to lift an injunction on President Trump’s mail-in ballot plan, saying it “threatens to silence” voters. “The right to vote is the foundation of our Democracy, and the Supreme Court’s decision allowing the President to move forward with this assault on that right is…
articles.body:
Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) bashed a recent Supreme Court decision to lift an injunction on President Trump’s mail-in ballot plan, saying it “threatens to silence” voters.

“The right to vote is the foundation of our Democracy, and the Supreme Court’s decision allowing the President to move forward with this assault on that right is an insult to the vision of our founders,” she said on social media .

The court’s conservative justices ruled in the case that the Democratic-led coalition of states — including the District of Columbia, California, Nevada and 21 others — sued too early , without ruling on the legality of Trump’s executive order.

The decision allowed the Department of Homeland Security to proceed with plans to create “state citizenship lists” composed of all eligible voters in a state.

Pelosi stated that she believes this order is “Trump’s attempt to seize control over Americans’ ability to vote by mail” and that it “threatens to silence their voices and must be challenged.”

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani blocked enforcement of the order, but the Supreme Court wrote in the emergency ruling that she had no authority to do so.

The court’s liberal minority said they would have kept the lower court’s hold in place, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, in a separate dissenting decision, calling the majority’s ruling a “ Kafkaesque nightmare .”

The executive order, signed in March, also directed the United States Postal Service to only issue mail-in ballots to people on the approved voter lists.

A separate injunction is still in place from the same lower court preventing the Postal Service from enforcing certain aspects of the executive order nationwide. It is still unclear if this case will be heard by the Supreme Court.

The Postal Service on Friday released an unpublished 95-page report , slated for an official release on Wednesday, that aligned with the executive order’s new eligibility guidelines.

The new policy gives states 60 days before the Nov. 3 midterms to notify the Postal Service if they intend to submit a list of eligible voters based on citizenship data. Only then will the Postal Service send mail-in or absentee ballots to the states’ respective residents.

The Postal Service on Friday released an unpublished 95-page report , slated for an official release on Wednesday, that aligned with the executive order’s new eligibility guidelines.

The new policy gives states 60 days before the Nov. 3 midterms to notify the Postal Service if they intend to submit a list of eligible voters based on citizenship data. Only then will the Postal Service send mail-in or absentee ballots to the states’ respective residents.

articles.title: Trump admin says Kennedy Center 'to be taken down' without renovations
articles.summary: Justice Department lawyers argued that without President Donald Trump’s support for renovating the Kennedy Center the “decrepit” venue “cannot be saved.”
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – Justice Department lawyers argued that without President Donald Trump 's support for renovating the Kennedy Center – including putting his name on the building and grounds – the "decrepit, dilapidated, crumbling" venue "cannot be saved."

Congress has approved $257 million for the project. But government lawyers argued that without Trump's additional fundraising aiming for more than $100 million, the work can't be completed.

The lawyers said a board member fighting the placement of his name on the building, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, should prefer that to having the building destroyed.

"The crisis is so acute that, without the Trump Administration, its people, and President Trump , the Center cannot survive, either structurally or financially," government lawyers said in a filing Aug. 25 . "The bottom line is this: Even Beatty should prefer a healthy, restored Center to a decaying hulk that is doomed to inevitable destruction or collapse."

Workers remove Trump's name from Kennedy Center building

Protesters wave a US flag and hold a sign reading "you're no JFK" as workers build scaffolding near the signage for the "Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts" in Washington, DC, on June 12, 2026. A US federal judge on June 12 rejected a bid by the board of the Kennedy Center and the Justice Department to halt the removal of President Donald Trump's name from the performing arts venue. District Judge Christopher Cooper, in a ruling last month, ordered Trump's name taken off the iconic building in the nation's capital by Friday.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper scheduled a hearing Aug. 27 to determine whether Trump's name should be blocked permanently from the building and grounds.

Cooper previously ordered the removal of Trump's name from the façade, after it was added during the renovation. And Cooper temporarily prevented the venue from closing during construction by ruling that the board had acted too hastily.

The board took a more deliberative process at an Aug. 13 meeting to decide to close the building for two years rather than work on renovations during partial closures over four years. The shorter schedule is projected to cost $285 million and the longer one $580 million.

"Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years," government lawyers said.

The board also voted to restore Trump's name to the façade and add it to the grounds.

The board voted to rename the building: "The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump."

If Trump's fundraising for the project reaches $100 million, the façade would read: "The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."

The board also voted to name the grounds beneath the venue "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

Government lawyers contend those moves don't violate the 1964 statute creating the center named for the late president, but merely recognize Trump for his contributions.

"Instead, the inscriptions only describe President Trump's role as the one responsible for the Center's renovation and restoration," the lawyers said.

But Beatty has called the naming moves "a breathtaking act of defiance" in filing an emergency motion asking Cooper to prevent Trump from restoring his name to the building.

"It bears emphasis: On the law, the latest renaming resolution is a breathtaking act of defiance," Beatty's filing said. "Moreover, the Board has determined to add the specific term 'Trump Kennedy Center' back onto the building – a jawdropping flouting of this Court's prohibition on use of that specific term."

articles.title: Air Force officer who called for Trump impeachment criminally charged
articles.summary: An Air Force officer who twice called for President Trump’s impeachment publicly on the steps of the Capitol has been criminally charged. Air Force Maj. Jason Watson is accused of breaking multiple military laws — allegedly committing three Article 88 violations for making “contemptuous” remarks about Trump, five Article 92 violations for disobeying orders and…
articles.body:
An Air Force officer who twice called for President Trump’s impeachment publicly on the steps of the Capitol has been criminally charged.

Air Force Maj. Jason Watson is accused of breaking multiple military laws — allegedly committing three Article 88 violations for making “contemptuous” remarks about Trump, five Article 92 violations for disobeying orders and two Article 133 violations for conduct unbecoming an officer, an Air Force spokesperson confirmed to The Hill.

“Maj. Watson will continue to be held in pre-trial confinement. Airmen are afforded the right to due process, and considered innocent until proven guilty, in accordance with the Uniform Code of Military Justice,” the Air Force spokesperson told The Hill.

“To protect the integrity of the judicial process, the privacy of personnel impacted by the alleged offense(s) and the rights of the accused, additional details regarding the evidence will not be released by the Air Force at this time,” the spokesperson added.

Article 88 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice criminalizes commissioned officers’ use of “contemptuous” words against the president, vice president, Congress and other key officials.

These charges are rare , as prosecutors must prove the words were explicitly “contemptuous” — meaning insulting, rude or disdainful — rather than protected or fair criticism, making convictions difficult.

Members of the U.S. military are strictly prohibited from participating in protests, marches or political demonstrations while wearing their uniform. Peaceful demonstrations are permitted on Capitol grounds, but a protester must be accompanied by a sitting lawmaker in order to speak openly on the steps of the Capitol.

Off-duty service members may attend peaceful protests or political events as spectators, but they must wear civilian clothes and ensure their personal views are not tied to their military status.

Last month, Watson was temporarily escorted by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to protest on the steps of the Capitol but was swiftly arrested after the lawmaker left the site.

Green has earned national media attention for protesting against Trump during a joint session of Congress, causing the representative’s removal. The Texas lawmaker filed impeachment articles against the president on Monday.

Meanwhile, Watson has remained unabashed in his pursuit of removing Trump from executive office.

He was arrested again last week and ordered into “pretrial confinement” for his early July protest on the Capitol, with authorities detaining the major shortly after he had informed his chain of command that he would “no longer be wearing his uniform.” The week of his arrest, he had again called for the president’s impeachment in an interview with CNN’s Erin Burnett.

“When the president of the United States orders military action against foreign countries — absent an emergency scenario where American interests are under imminent dire threats, as was done with Venezuela, Cuba and Iran — that’s an unconstitutional usurpation of Congress’s authority and a violation of the War Powers Clause,” Watson originally told bystanders in July.

“These violations resulted in the deaths of 13 service members and injuries of hundreds more. For this, the president and vice president must be impeached, convicted and removed,” he added.

articles.title: Canada to place retaliatory tariffs on US goods
articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Business & Economy newsletter {beacon} Business & Economy Business & Economy The Big Story Canada strikes back with retaliatory tariffs Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of American products as high as 50 percent Tuesday, just days after the collapse of negotiations between the two countries. © Justin Tang/The Canadian…
articles.body:
Canada strikes back with retaliatory tariffs

Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of American products as high as 50 percent Tuesday, just days after the collapse of negotiations between the two countries.

Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada will match the U.S.’s tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.” The tariffs would take effect Sept. 8.

He said the 15 percent, 25 percent and 50 percent tariffs will be on $27.6 billion of imports from the U.S.

“For each product, our tariff will match the American tariff on the same type of Canadian good,” he said.

Arguably the biggest measure is Canada doubling its tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum to 50 percent to match the 50 percent the U.S. put on Canadian steel and aluminum.

“Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses, and communities across our nation,” Champagne said of the U.S. tariffs. “Canada must respond, and today we are in a proportionate, targeted, and strategic way.”

He said the countertariffs “are designed primarily to provide protection for Canadian industries impacted by the U.S. tariffs and allow them to compete against U.S. products in the Canadian market.”

Canada released a list of over 700 items that will be targeted with tariffs ranging from live fish, frozen fish, cheese, some apparel, carpets and metal products made of steel or aluminum, among others.

The U.S.’s 50 percent tariffs went into effect on Saturday across over $20 billion of Canadian imports after negotiations collapsed late Friday.

articles.body:
President Trump’s pick to succeed term-limited Gov. Kevin Stitt in Oklahoma is duking it out in a Tuesday GOP runoff for the party’s nod.

Mike Mazzei, a former state senator and state budget secretary, is facing off against state Attorney General Gentner Drummond. Trump has called Drummond a “fake Republican,” ripping the candidate for not having an opinion “on the BOGUS IMPEACHMENT of a young and very handsome gentleman, named, President Donald J. Trump (ME!).”

Drummond narrowly led Mazzei in the initial June 16 primary by about 1,100 votes. The winner of Tuesday’s runoff is the favorite to win the November election in the ruby red state.

Polls close at 8 p.m. EDT. Follow Decision Desk HQ’s live results below.

articles.body:
Voters in Georgia’s 13th Congressional District are at the polls Tuesday for a special election to fill late Rep. David Scott’s (D) seat through the rest of the year.

Scott’s daughter, Marcye Scott, and Everton Blair, a former Gwinnett County board of education member, advanced from the runoff after no candidate secured more than half of the vote on July 28. Both candidates are Democrats.

Democrat Jasmine Clark, a state lawmaker, won the Democratic primary for the full term in the blue district. She will face Republican Jonathan Chavez in November.

Polls close at 7 p.m. EDT. Follow Decision Desk HQ’s live results below.

articles.title: Report kept from residents now revealed, shows toxic levels in East Palestine
articles.summary: East Palestine residents participating in a class-action settlement say lawyers suppressed their expert’s environmental report to convince them to take the money.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Shortly after the 2023 train derailment and burning of vinyl chloride in East Palestine, Ohio, renowned exposure-warnings expert and industrial hygienist Stephen Petty tested the soil and water for residents.

Petty had been hired by class-action attorneys as their testing expert.

When the attorneys negotiated a $600 million settlement with Norfolk Southern , they did not release Petty’s results — even to their own clients.

Nexstar’s NewsNation has obtained those results and interviewed Petty.

Never-released report shows contamination, Petty says

Petty told NewsNation there are carcinogens in the soil in East Palestine and that they are “above screening levels, which means you can’t walk away from it.”

Petty said his testing data, and other data he analyzed, show dioxins and PAHs ( polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons ), some of the most carcinogenic compounds on the planet, at elevated levels.

The levels are above cancer-screening levels set by the EPA , which requires further testing and analysis.

“Somewhere between 50% and 70% of the data points, whether they be for dioxins or PAHs, exceeded screening levels” for cancer, Petty said.

“You have to do something. You have to do further analysis to see what needs to be done from a remediation standpoint. And you also have to do further analysis to determine what it means for people in that environment,” Petty said. “There is a problem there.”

Independent testing expert Scott Smith also came to test on his own. He said he found elevated levels of dioxin, too. Smith and Petty are both whistleblowers represented by the Government Accountability Project.

“It’s astounding in that it was suppressed,” he said. “Forty-nine percent of the testing exceeds the EPA cancer screening level. Seventy percent of Stephen Petty’s data and analysis shows polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons above the EPA cancer screening level.”

“It lines up exactly with my data,” he said.

Their own lawyers kept the data from them, residents say

Residents said the story they got from the attorneys in the class-action lawsuit was very different.

“They told me that in my home, basically, that the numbers didn’t support the outcome of the $600 million,” resident Linda Murphy said. “The numbers weren’t bad enough. Murphy shared an audio recording she said was from a meeting with the lawyers. In the recording, the speakers can be heard saying, “The data is nowhere near as bad as we thought it was going to be when this first happened.”

The speaker also said, “It’s almost unprovably bad, specifically for medical monitoring, showing that people have been exposed at a certain level so as to require 10, 20 years of diagnostic testing. Virtually unprovable for any long-term chronic future illness like cancer.”

They also said, “The chemicals did not persist long enough at quantities that will expose people over the necessary period of time to produce long-term health effects that are associated directly to this exposure.”

Austin Druckenbrod, another East Palestine resident, said he asked the lawyers directly about the tests: “I asked him when I was concerned about the testing they had, that it may not have been the truth. And he said, ‘They’re hacks. And Scott Smith doesn’t know what he’s talking about. And neither does Stephen Petty,’ And he said, ‘Don’t believe them.’”

NewsNation has reviewed text messages that appear to back up what Druckenbrod told us.

Though the attorneys didn’t share Petty’s results with residents, they did enlist a toxicologist to film a video that played for the residents.

The video was filmed by Dr. Arch “Chip” Carson, M.D., PhD., who is listed on the video as principal of Environmental Medicine Consultants. He is associated with multiple universities, including Ohio State University , the University of Cincinnati and the University of Texas School of Public Health.

In one part of the video, Dr. Carson said, “The levels that people were exposed to in the community were so small that we don’t expect any kinds of cancers or health effects to have resulted from those. Petty told NewsNation, “The argument that there is nothing to see here is factually false. Multiple people saying there’s nothing to see here … are just flat out lying or are wrong.”

Mindy Bish is an attorney now representing East Palestine residents who are trying to rescind their participation in the settlement.

“Arch Carson told everyone that there was, that he would expect no cancers as a result of this exposure. No cancers. And there are cancers developing almost every week in East Palestine and someone dying of cancer almost every month,” Bish told NewsNation.

“These attorneys told them that the Stephen Petty information would not support the claims. And that is not true,” Bish said. “My first impressions when I saw Stephen Petty’s results was this is fraudulent, this is concealment, this is manipulation.”

Neither Carson nor the attorneys in the class-action settlement have responded to requests for comment from NewsNation.

Nearly 90 residents are seeking to rescind their participation in the settlement.

In part, their motion alleged “Substantial evidence of fraud and misrepresentation by class counsel, who concealed critical expert findings about health risks while inducing class members to sign personal injury releases in exchange for inadequate personal injury payments.”

In April, a judge denied their effort to reopen the settlement. They have filed an appeal alleging that class counsel’s own expert, Petty, held opinions materially adverse to the settlement that were not disclosed before opt-in.

“I believe I was manipulated,” Druckenbord said. “I believe there was fraud. And I have the future, and my future is going to rely on proving the bad actors were wrong.”

articles.title: GOP election law expert: Many more ‘low propensity voters in Republican Party’ after Trump mail-in voting ruling
articles.summary: Election law attorney Ben Ginsberg said Monday that President Trump’s executive order imposing restrictions on mail-in voting will largely impact Republican voters. “One thing is, I think you’re going to see some blowback from Republicans in the coming weeks, because after all, Republicans are the older party and older folks like to vote by mail.…
articles.body:
Election law attorney Ben Ginsberg said Monday that President Trump’s executive order imposing restrictions on mail-in voting will largely impact Republican voters.

“One thing is, I think you’re going to see some blowback from Republicans in the coming weeks, because after all, Republicans are the older party and older folks like to vote by mail. They’re the rural party,” Ginsberg said during a Monday appearance on CNN’s “The Source.”

“And certainly vote by mail is important to people in rural areas. And thanks to Donald Trump, there are many more low propensity voters in the Republican Party,” he added.

Ginsberg has served as counsel to the Republican National Committee, National Republican Senatorial Committee, National Republican Congressional Committee and Republican Governors Association.

His Monday comments follow the Supreme Court’s decision to issue an unsigned order in which the majority determined that Democratic states’ legal challenges to Trump’s executive order overhauling mail-in voting were premature.

“The States lack standing to challenge. … It does nothing to them,” the majority opinion says .

One of the clauses in the president’s order would require states to provide a list of eligible voters to the U.S. Postal Service for distribution and prevent the agency from distributing ballots to those excluded from the list.

“Section 3 orders the Postal Service to initiate the process of proposing a rule that might bind the States in the future. It is not a proposed rule, let alone a final rule,” the majority opinion says.

“And it imposes no legal requirements on the States (or, for that matter, on anyone outside the Executive Branch),” it continues.

Trump’s order has twice been blocked by lower courts and has faced pushback from both Republicans and Democrats alike.

“Republican operatives in the states know that putting up those barriers to that part of the Republican base makes Republican turnout less likely,” Ginsburg said Monday.

“So this is kind of a flawed political strategy wrapped in a rather vocally charged policy from the president,” he added.

Despite criticism, the Trump administration moved forward with an appeal Tuesday to lift the nationwide block on the executive order restricting mail-in ballots.

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library says it will keep sending free books to kids. Here’s how to sign up
articles.summary: The Imagination Library will continue sending books to eligible children in Parton’s absence, a spokesperson for the Dollywood Company confirmed.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Dolly Parton’s legacy will continue not only through her music, but through her foundation that sends free books to children in the U.S. and four other countries, regardless of their family’s financial situation.

Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library first launched in 1995 as a way to send free books to young children in Sevier County, Tennessee, where Parton grew up. It has since grown immensely, and now serves 1 in 6 children in the U.S. who are under the age of 5.

The Imagination Library will continue sending books to eligible children in Parton’s absence, a spokesperson for the Dollywood Company confirmed to Nexstar.

Families who sign up get a free, high-quality, age-appropriate book mailed to them every month.

Who qualifies for the Imagination Library?

Kids can start receiving books in the mail as soon as they’re born and until they turn 5. The program fully covers the cost of books and postage, regardless of the family’s income.

The Dolly Parton Imagination Library teams up with local partners to send books out, so you’ll need to make sure they’re operating in your area in order to start receiving them.

You can check if the program is available in your area here . If you enter your ZIP code and the Imagination Library program is operating in your district, you can sign up to receive a free, high-quality book in the mail every month. You may be directed to your county or city’s library website to complete registration.

The Dollywood Company encouraged people to donate to the Imagination Library as a way to honor the late country singer. Parton’s family announced her death Tuesday. She was 80 years old.

“When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams,” Parton once said, according to the Imagination Library website. “They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer. The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”
