articles.title: El-Sayed distances from Piker amid high-stakes Senate race
articles.summary: Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is taking steps to distance his Senate campaign from far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who’s facing blowback for suggesting that American Jews’ support for Israel could make antisemitism worse. El-Sayed, who faces Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.) this fall in a must-win Senate race, had raised the hackles of some fellow Democrats…
articles.body:
Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is taking steps to distance his Senate campaign from far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who’s facing blowback for suggesting that American Jews’ support for Israel could make antisemitism worse.

El-Sayed, who faces Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.) this fall in a must-win Senate race, had raised the hackles of some fellow Democrats for his campaign trail appearances with Piker, who’s pushed further into the national spotlight as progressive candidates court his massive, young audience.

But Piker’s latest comments, which add to a string of controversial remarks, are putting El-Sayed on defense in the critical battleground, prompting the Democrat to stress that “nobody” outside his team speaks for the Senate campaign.

Some Democrats, however, were annoyed by the distraction in such a critical time in the race, when El-Sayed needs to be appealing to a wide swath of voters.

“It’s just off message,” Democratic strategist Steve Schale said. “Besides being reprehensible in their own right, El-Sayed has to spend valuable campaign time reacting to Piker’s incendiary comments instead of talking about how to make things cost less and other issues Michigan voters care about.

“There’s no world where Hasan Piker’s comments are anything but a net negative for any candidate trying to get 50 plus 1 in a battleground race.”

Other strategists agree, making the case that the comments could hurt him with the electorate.

“El-Sayed would rather not respond to Piker’s comments while also running against his Republican opponent,” said Basil Smikle, a Democratic strategist. “Defending his left and his right flank is dizzying for him and a potential turnoff to voters.”

In the midterm home stretch, the stakes are high for El-Sayed, who defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens (D) by less than a percentage point in a closely watched Democratic primary earlier this month.

The progressive’s win in purple Michigan added to a string of left-wing wins in primaries this cycle, offering a new data point for Democrats searching for the best path forward after losses in 2024.

Such proxy-war primaries, though, have spotlighted Democratic fears that more progressive candidates could be a liability in the general election — as Republicans seek to paint the party at large as too far to the left.

El-Sayed’s association with Piker had already become a hurdle in the primary , a costly contest that was dominated by issues around electability, outside spending and support for Israel. Stevens told Jewish Insider in April that Piker is “the exact opposite of someone I’d be campaigning with.” And state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who later dropped out of the race, compared Piker to far-right influencer Nick Fuentes, an avowed antisemite.

With millions of followers on YouTube, Instagram and social platform X, Piker boasts a large online following that could give progressive candidates like El-Sayed a leg up — but experts say it could also help fuel Republicans’ rhetoric about the race.

The latest controversy comes after Piker suggested in a recent Twitch stream that if “Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s going to come around and take action. … Not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.”

Rogers jumped in to condemn Piker’s comments and tie them to El-Sayed, suggesting the streamer was the Democrat’s “running mate.”

“More calls for violence coming out of the El-Sayed campaign … Here is his running mate, Hasan Piker, saying that if AMERICAN JEWS support Israel, they will be violently targeted because of it,” Rogers wrote on X.

Piker defended himself, saying on X that “this isn’t a call for violence” and that “falsely tying israel to jewish people IS increasing antisemitism.” El-Sayed also weighed in, putting distance between his campaign and Piker’s platform.

“My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters,” El-Sayed said in a statement on social media. “Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk.”

“But I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople,” he added, suggesting that “politicians and pundits” are trying “to make this race about a Twitch streamer.”

Activist David Hogg had a similar take, saying over the weekend that the media’s focus on Piker is “kind of weird” as “the median voter knows nothing about” the streamer.

Stevens, who has rallied behind El-Sayed since losing the primary, had said earlier this month that it “certainly makes sense” for El-Sayed to “get rid” of his affiliation with Piker.

Piker’s recent comments are the latest in a history of controversial statements, including his 2019 remark that “America deserved 9/11” as blowback against U.S. military campaigns — though he’s recently said he could have better phrased the claim.

Republicans say the totality of the remarks — coupled with some of El-Sayed’s statements — are bad news for his campaign.

“This race will be determined by what the conversation is about,” Republican strategist Doug Heye said. “El-Sayed’s bizarre no-name Piker statement and really out there Fox News interview put the spotlight exactly where he doesn’t want it – on him.”

GOP strategist Brian Seitchik, said it was “politically convenient” for El-Sayed to distance himself from Piker. “Now that he’s in the general election, El-Sayed has suddenly found the courage to distance himself from proud American hater Hasan Piker,” Seitchik said. “But a change in campaign strategy doesn’t erase the record of reality that both men are enthusiastic antisemites.”

“Michigan voters will decide between a mainstream-normi like Mike Rogers or a hater with a long record of hyper troubling rhetoric about Israel and the Jewish community,” he added. “A charming delivery doesn’t make extreme views any less extreme.”

Michigan Democratic strategist Adrian Hemond said El-Sayed “needs leftists like Hasan Piker to think nicely of him” to support his apparent theory of the case that “he can remake the electorate by bringing more progressive voters” to the polls.

But Piker’s controversies don’t help El-Sayed stay in a positive light, Hemond said. He argued that more distance from Piker and a message that focuses more on the competition with Republicans than on the future for Democrats are El-Sayed’s best path forward in the race, which is critical for Democrats in their fight for Senate control.

Cook Political Report considers the race a toss-up this fall, while Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) now views the race as leaning toward Democrats, a step away from toss-up territory. The latest DDHQ polling averages signal El-Sayed and Rogers are in a dead heat, taking turns in the lead over the last two months.

If Republicans win the Michigan seat in November, though, DDHQ estimates that Republicans jump to an 86 percent chance of holding the upper chamber.

“In an environment like this, a Democrat should be running away with this race, both because the president is deeply unpopular and because Republicans basically don’t win U.S. Senate elections in Michigan,” Hemond said.

David Dulio, a political science professor at Oakland University in Michigan, suggested that El-Sayed’s distance from Piker signals he understands the high stakes and is gearing up for the general.

He pointed out that El-Sayed’s association with Piker was helpful during the primary.

“I mean, he went with Piker to Ann Arbor and East Lansing, and they packed the joints. And it doesn’t surprise me now, that he’s looking to, you know, pump the brakes a little bit. I would expect that. It’s a candidate transitioning from primary to general,” Dulio said.

“I think all the concerns are well founded because Michigan is not New York City,” he said of the fear that the far-left brand could be a riskier bet in November. “That brand of progressivism it’s going to be a tough sell in Michigan.”

Some other Democrats conceded that Piker’s comments were largely unhelpful, and as Democratic strategist Eddie Vale put it, “if those individual diversions start to add up, then it can become a problem.”

Still, Vale added, “Ultimately this election is going to be decided on [President] Trump and his cratering economy.

“So random distractions aren’t going to be fatal to anyone’s campaign in and of themselves,” he said.

He argued that more distance from Piker and a message that focuses more on the competition with Republicans than on the future for Democrats are El-Sayed’s best path forward in the race, which is critical for Democrats in their fight for Senate control.

Cook Political Report considers the race a toss-up this fall, while Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) now views the race as leaning toward Democrats, a step away from toss-up territory. The latest DDHQ polling averages signal El-Sayed and Rogers are in a dead heat, taking turns in the lead over the last two months.
If Republicans win the Michigan seat in November, though, DDHQ estimates that Republicans jump to an 86 percent chance of holding the upper chamber.

“In an environment like this, a Democrat should be running away with this race, both because the president is deeply unpopular and because Republicans basically don’t win U.S. Senate elections in Michigan,” Hemond said.
David Dulio, a political science professor at Oakland University in Michigan, suggested that El-Sayed’s distance from Piker signals he understands the high stakes and is gearing up for the general.
He pointed out that El-Sayed’s association with Piker was helpful during the primary.

“I mean, he went with Piker to Ann Arbor and East Lansing, and they packed the joints. And it doesn’t surprise me now, that he’s looking to, you know, pump the brakes a little bit. I would expect that. It’s a candidate transitioning from primary to general,” Dulio said.

“I think all the concerns are well founded because Michigan is not New York City,” he said of the fear that the far-left brand could be a riskier bet in November. “That brand of progressivism it’s going to be a tough sell in Michigan.”

Some other Democrats conceded that Piker’s comments were largely unhelpful, and as Democratic strategist Eddie Vale put it, “if those individual diversions start to add up, then it can become a problem.”
Still, Vale added, “Ultimately this election is going to be decided on [President] Trump and his cratering economy.
“So random distractions aren’t going to be fatal to anyone’s campaign in and of themselves,” he said.

articles.title: DOJ warns Kennedy Center could be knocked down if renovations blocked
articles.summary: The Trump administration said it may need to demolish the Kennedy Center if a plan to close the building for two years as part of a controversial renovation...
articles.body:
The Trump administration said it may need to demolish the Kennedy Center if a plan to close the building for two years as part of a controversial renovation project pushed by President Trump and the organization's board of trustees is blocked by a federal judge.

In a Tuesday court filing , the Justice Department said the center's "dangerously dilapidated, outdated, and decrepit" conditions, in addition to millions in financial losses, put the living memorial to President John F. Kennedy in a "financial and structural death spiral" that will require it to close for renovations.

"Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years," lawyers for the federal government wrote.

There are no official existing plans to tear down the almost 55-year-old performing arts center. But the warning could raise the stakes in a monthslong legal dispute over the center, which Mr. Trump and his handpicked board of trustees have sought to overhaul.

Lawyers for Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, a board member who filed a lawsuit over the changes to the Kennedy Center, skewered Tuesday's filing.

"This is a not-so-subtle threat to demolish the Kennedy Center if the President doesn't get his way," said attorneys Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky. "This is unconscionable, it is unbecoming of the Department of Justice to even put this in a filing, and we will answer in court."

The Kennedy Center's board voted earlier this month to close the center and add Mr. Trump's name to its facade, marking its second attempt to make those sweeping changes.

Less than three months earlier, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper barred the center's closure and ordered Mr. Trump's name to be removed from the building, ruling in Beatty's favor. Construction crews removed the president's name from the facade, but the front portico of the building has been covered by a construction tarp since then, concealing most of its name.

In his May ruling, Cooper found the board was "derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center" by moving to close the institution, calling the decision to cease operations during renovations "ill-informed and seemingly preordained." Cooper said he was not "categorically" barring the center from closing its doors or moving forward with construction, but wanted to ensure the board followed "certain minimum requirements imposed by law."

During a mid-August meeting that Mr. Trump called into, the Kennedy Center's board approved closure plans yet again. The board also voted in favor of adding the phrase "Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump" to the end of the center's formal name, the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, and moved to rename the physical site as the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza." Prior to Cooper's ruling, the board had attempted to rename the organization altogether as the Trump-Kennedy Center.

In court filings last week , the Trump administration said it will pause its latest round of planned changes to the building until Sept. 8.

Last week, Beatty once again asked the court to block the president's name from being added to the building, calling it "déjà vu all over again." Beatty's lawyers have argued that only Congress, not the Kennedy Center's board, may change the name of the building.

"In a new and breathtaking act of defiance of Congress and of this Court, Defendants have voted to return President Trump's name to the Kennedy Center's façade. This time, Trump's name will appear on the building's front portico not once, but twice," Beatty's lawyers wrote, calling the repeated additions of Mr. Trump's name to the building "a transparent effort to rename the Center in President Trump's honor."

Cooper is set to hear arguments from lawyers for Beatty on Thursday.

In response, the Justice Department defended the center's board of trustees, arguing that the resolution is "completely lawful," and accused Beatty of a "hyper-partisan effort to oppose any recognition of President Trump's contributions to the Center."

"Even Beatty should prefer a healthy, restored Center to a decaying hulk that is doomed to inevitable destruction or collapse," the Justice Department wrote. "The Court should allow the Board and President Trump to bring the Center back to a level of greatness far higher than it has ever had before. This would be the fitting tribute that President Kennedy so well deserves."

articles.title: Hegseth’s Army Purges Have Undermined Military Leadership on Iran
articles.summary: The extent to which Trump’s “Secretary of War” has damaged the United States’ military capability is even worse than previously thought.
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's decision to fire numerous top generals has put America's military between a rock and a hard place in its war against Iran.

The Army has been without a chief of staff since Hegseth fired General Randy George in April; he has forced out at least three senior officers that were believed to be in the running to be George's replacement, according to current and former officials that spoke with The New York Times .

All in all, Hegseth has forced out at least half a dozen senior officers, according to inside sources that spoke with the Times , who say this purge has damaged the service's expertise and has eroded its top ranks.

Those affected include General James Mingus, the Army vice chief of staff that Hegseth forced out last year with little explanation, and General David Hodne, whom Hegseth hired and then fired just eight months later.

Other axed officers include Major General William Green, General Christopher Donahue, and General James Slife, the Air Force vice chief of staff.

General CQ Brown Jr. was also fired from his position as the chairman of the Joint Chiefs in the early weeks of Donald Trump's second term, and General David Allvin retired early last fall.

Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll, the Army's top civilian leader, is also believed to be on his way out in the coming months, according to the Times , which reported that Driscoll has already moved out of the large family house he was renting outside Washington.

"Hollowing out the most battle-tested and most lethal, proven leaders in a time of war means troops are less safe and we're less likely to win," Representative Pat Ryan, Democrat of New York and a former Army intelligence officer, told the daily newspaper. "We're doing generational damage to the sense that the military is an apolitical trusted organization that swears an oath to the Constitution, not to a president."

Hegseth's decision to undermine top military leadership has left a definitive vacuum in the highest echelons of the Army. At the time of Hegseth's confirmation, there were 10 four-star generals on active duty. Now, there are just five—the smallest number to lead the service in years.

Meanwhile, the Army's Middle East bases have been battered by Iran's seemingly endless supply of cheap drones since late February. The conflict has so far killed at least 18 U.S. servicemembers and wounded more than 776 others. It has also taken an enormous toll on daily life in the U.S., inflaming the cost of practically everything as shipping companies contend with rising oil costs.

articles.title: Map Shows Senate Battlegrounds Hit Hardest by Canada Tariffs
articles.summary: Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods Tuesday after its negotiations with Washington collapsed.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada has created a new political challenge for Republican candidates in several of the year's most closely watched Senate races.

Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods Tuesday after its negotiations with Washington collapsed, following the administration's decision to raise tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian imports.

Economists have warned this is likely to raise costs and disrupt supply chains, especially in several competitive Senate battleground states that may decide control of the chamber in November's midterm elections.

"With this latest round of tariffs being imposed on Canada, focus will once again shift to the effects of them on Americans' wallets, especially in states like Michigan, Ohio, and Alaska, where Canada remains a pivotal trading partner," Alex Beene, a financial literacy instructor for the University of Tennessee at Martin, told Newsweek .

Democrats' path to reclaiming the Senate runs through a mix of traditional battlegrounds and Republican-held states including Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas, while Michigan is one of the most competitive open-seat races in the country. Maine is also one of Democrats' best pickup opportunities.

The U.S. and Canada have one of the world's largest trading relationships, supporting auto and agriculture industries as well as seafood, forestry and energy.

Many of the states with competitive Senate contests are particularly exposed because Canada is a major export market or a critical supplier of raw materials and components for their region.

Any prolonged tariff standoff could affect jobs and consumer prices right before voters head to the polls.

Senate Battleground States Most Exposed to Canada Tariffs

The Senate battleground states that are most exposed to the impact of Canada tariffs include:

"Nationally, the main issue, as is the case in most elections, comes down to one word: cost," Kevin Thompson, the CEO of 9i Capital Group and the host of the 9innings podcast, told Newsweek . "No one wants to pay more for goods and services, yet that is exactly what is happening."

Michigan: Auto Industry in the Crosshairs

Michigan is perhaps the clearest example of a state caught between economics and politics.

The state sends roughly one-third of its exports to Canada, and its automotive sector depends on supply chains that routinely cross the border multiple times before a vehicle is assembled.

Canada also targeted products tied to steel, aluminum and manufacturing in its tariff retaliation.

"We often hide behind the word 'inflation,' but that does not tell the entire story. If tariffs become the norm, prices will continue to rise as those additional costs are passed on to the end consumer in the form of higher prices," Thompson said.

The state's open Senate race is one of the nation's most competitive following the retirement of Democratic Senator Gary Peters. Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed has already sought to make tariffs a campaign issue.

"Trump is escalating a trade war with Canada for his own vanity," El-Sayed said on social media, while criticizing Republican opponent Mike Rogers.

Ohio: Manufacturing and Agriculture at Risk

Ohio exported approximately $21.8 billion worth of goods to Canada, making its northern neighbor the state's largest international trading partner, experts say.

"The reality is if residents of these states start to see the ramifications of these tariffs in the coming months, it absolutely could sway some of their votes," Beene said.

Right now, Ohio faces exposure through its manufacturing, steel, aluminum and industrial supply chains, and agricultural producers could also be affected if the retaliatory tariffs persist.

The Senate contest between Republican incumbent Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown has been viewed as one of Democrats' best opportunities in Trump country. Moving forward, tariffs could become a particularly sensitive issue in industrial communities where businesses rely on Canadian customers or imports.

Iowa: Farmer and Farm Equipment Pressure

Iowa's economy is also deeply connected to North American trade through agriculture and farm manufacturing.

The Canadian tariff retaliation has targeted products such as farm equipment and dairy-related goods, and Iowa sends a substantial amount of its exports to Canada and Mexico.

Amid the tariffs, the Senate race between Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic challenger Josh Turek has become increasingly competitive.

Few Senate candidates have been more outspoken about the tariffs than Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins.

"Imposing new tariffs on Canada is a mistake," Collins said while campaigning Monday, warning that Maine industries including lobster, blueberries and lumber could suffer.

Maine's economy is uniquely tied to Canada through forestry, seafood, tourism and agriculture.

Collins is facing one of the toughest reelection campaigns of her career against Democrat Troy Jackson as many Democrats view this race as their top pickup opportunity.

Canada is a major market for Alaska seafood products, and retaliatory tariffs targeting fish and seafood could create challenges for exporters already dealing with broader industry pressures.

Democratic former Representative Mary Peltola is currently attempting to unseat Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in one of the country's most competitive races.

This could cause Alaska to emerge as an unexpected battleground despite Trump's strong 2024 performance there, and the trade dispute could become a major talking point if seafood processors experience slowing demand.

Texas may have the largest absolute economic exposure because of its enormous trade volume, even if Canada accounts for a smaller share of the state's economy than in Maine or Michigan.

So far, the Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico has become far more competitive than many commentators expected. Several forecasters have even shifted the race toward a toss-up status as Democrats attempt to move even traditionally Republican states.

If the trade dispute begins affecting jobs or consumer prices, Democrats could argue that the tariffs are worsening economic pressures already facing households.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs are scheduled to take effect September 8, so businesses and consumers could begin feeling the impact just weeks before voters cast ballots.

With Senate control potentially coming down to a handful of races in Michigan, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Alaska and Texas, the economic consequences of the Canada tariff battle may soon become a major campaign issue.

"The reality is that politics has become increasingly ideological. For some voters, those cost increases may not matter because the policy aligns with who or what they support. For others, however, cost will be a major concern when they go to the polls," Thompson said.

"And tariffs increase costs. That is simply Econ 101."

articles.title: Clinton-appointed judge triggers appeal after blocking key voter citizenship law
articles.summary: Frank LaRose vows to appeal after a Clinton-appointed judge blocked Ohio's voter registration citizenship proof law, citing federal conflicts.
articles.body:
A Clinton-appointed judge in Ohio is blocking the implementation of an Ohio law that requires voting registrants to provide photo ID proof of their citizenship before enrollment.

In a decision delivered on Tuesday, Judge Solomon Oliver Jr. stayed the law, citing what he saw as a conflict with federal requirements.

"The court grants plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction … from relying on House Bill 54's amendment to require any driver's license or renewal to produce documentary proof of citizenship before offering the opportunity to register to vote," Oliver wrote.

The decision is just the latest development in the national debate over state-level voting requirements designed to prevent non-citizens from participating in U.S. elections — and how far those requirements can go without overarching federal reforms.

Federal Appeals Court Restores Texas Mail Ballot Id Requirements In Major Election Integrity Ruling

Most immediately, the decision means that voter registrants in Ohio can once again enroll without a passport, a current driver's license, a certification of naturalization , or a birth certificate.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose announced on Tuesday that his office plans to appeal the decision.

"We strongly disagree with that decision, and I've asked our legal team to file an immediate appeal. I will vigorously defend our legal authority to safeguard our voter rolls and protect the integrity of Ohio's elections," LaRose said in a statement.

In the case of Red Wine & Blue v. the Ohio Secretary of State, the court was asked to weigh whether requirements under the new Ohio law conflict with the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), also known as the "Motor Voter Act."

That law, passed in 1993 under the Clinton administration, instructs states to give voters the opportunity to register to vote using the same information they use when applying for a driver's license. The bill was originally intended to increase voter participation.

New Jersey Removes 6,600 People From Voter Rolls Who Were Eligible To Cast A Ballot For 2024 Election

It states that "the voter registration application portion … for a driver's license may not require any information that duplicates information required in the driver's license portion of the form."

Notably, the NVRA doesn't explicitly prohibit states from requiring proof of citizenship . But because virtually all driver's license forms ask about citizenship status, Oliver believes further proof amounts to redundancy.

He laid out his view in Tuesday's decision.

"As the rest of Ohio's voter registration scheme demonstrates, election officials do not need documentary proof of citizenship to assess a voter registration applicant's citizenship because signed attestation of citizenship is enough," Oliver wrote.

LaRose, the secretary of state, disagreed. He cited instances of known voter fraud that have escaped detection because of the current enforcement mechanisms.

Mexican National Convicted Of Illegally Voting In Us After False Citizenship Claims Faces Removal: Dhs

"Earlier this year, an Ohio woman admitted to voting illegally as a lawful permanent resident in 2018 because, according to the judge in the case, 'a [Bureau of Motor Vehicles] clerk, a government official, told her to register.' The court found her not guilty by reason of entrapment. The judge specifically noted that the voter admitted she knew she was not a citizen when she voted, but he found that the BMV employee misled her into violating the law by implying she was eligible to vote." " The Franklin County case proves it's not enough to just have a person's attestation," LaRose added. "Ohio has a constitutional requirement to ensure that only U.S. citizens are voting in our elections."

It states that "the voter registration application portion … for a driver's license may not require any information that duplicates information required in the driver's license portion of the form."

Notably, the NVRA doesn't explicitly prohibit states from requiring proof of citizenship . But because virtually all driver's license forms ask about citizenship status, Oliver believes further proof amounts to redundancy.
He laid out his view in Tuesday's decision.

"As the rest of Ohio's voter registration scheme demonstrates, election officials do not need documentary proof of citizenship to assess a voter registration applicant's citizenship because signed attestation of citizenship is enough," Oliver wrote.
LaRose, the secretary of state, disagreed. He cited instances of known voter fraud that have escaped detection because of the current enforcement mechanisms.
Mexican National Convicted Of Illegally Voting In Us After False Citizenship Claims Faces Removal: Dhs

"Earlier this year, an Ohio woman admitted to voting illegally as a lawful permanent resident in 2018 because, according to the judge in the case, 'a [Bureau of Motor Vehicles] clerk, a government official, told her to register.' The court found her not guilty by reason of entrapment. The judge specifically noted that the voter admitted she knew she was not a citizen when she voted, but he found that the BMV employee misled her into violating the law by implying she was eligible to vote." " The Franklin County case proves it's not enough to just have a person's attestation," LaRose added. "Ohio has a constitutional requirement to ensure that only U.S. citizens are voting in our elections."

articles.body:
Paramount’s Warner Bros. bid barrels toward antitrust trial

Paramount’s bid to acquire fellow entertainment giant Warner Brothers Discovery (WBD) has been mired in controversy and drew a lawsuit from critics who argue the deal is bad for the movie-making and media business.

As David Ellison , the company’s top executive and an ally of President Trump, wages a public relations and legal defense campaign advocating for the merger, a Democrat-led suit seeking to stop it appears likely headed for a jury trial in California next spring.

The case took a dramatic turn this week, when California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) called off a planned settlement meeting over what he said were leaks orchestrated by Paramount publicizing details of previous meetings between the two sides, tainting the negotiating process.

The company and state government have been trading barbs in court and the media for weeks, with Paramount’s top legal officer saying earlier this month the company was considering leaving its headquarters in Southern California if Bonta does not drop his suit.

The Hill’s Dominick Mastrangelo breaks down the latest here .

articles.title: Mark Carney, the former central banker who said 'no' to Trump
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is more seasoned as a banker than a politician but has shown a confident touch in standing up to US President Donald Trum...
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is more seasoned as a banker than a politician but has shown a confident touch in standing up to US President Donald Trump and navigating a trade war that threatens his nation's economy.

"We are masters in our own house," the prime minister said on Saturday, just hours after breaking off trade talks with the United States and ordering his negotiators back to Ottawa.

Despite the risks this decision poses to Canada, which is heavily dependent on exports to the US, Carney can boast of broad support, with 76 percent of the public praising his stance toward Washington, according to a weekend poll.

"Mark Carney has the means to achieve his ambitions because the country is behind him," says Genevieve Tellier, a professor of political science at the University of Ottawa.

After Washington slapped Canada with 50-percent duties, Canada on Tuesday announced counter-tariffs of its own.

Former head of Canada's central bank, Carney, 61, was not known for his charisma -- unlike his flamboyant predecessor Justin Trudeau, from the same Liberal Party -- but has nevertheless managed to kindle a patriotic flame among Canadians weary of American attacks.

It was trade tension with the United States that propelled him to power -- two months after Trump began his second term -- as Canadians saw him as a protector of their economy.

Replacing Trudeau as leader of his party and the government in March 2025, he won a general election a month later, to everyone's surprise.

"He transformed into a politician quite quickly; it was a surprise," said Tellier.

A blunt speech Carney gave at January's World Economic Forum marked a turning point for him on the international stage.

Declaring that the world was in the midst of a "rupture in the world order," he called on middle powers like Canada to unite.

"If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he said.

The speech sent a message that Carney was positioning himself "as an international leader with a different, credible vision," Tellier said.

After studying at Harvard and Oxford, Mark Carney made his fortune as an investment banker at Goldman Sachs in New York, London, Tokyo and Toronto.

In 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis, he was appointed governor of the Bank of Canada by a conservative prime minister, Stephen Harper.

Five years later, he was chosen by a conservative British prime minister, David Cameron, to head the Bank of England, becoming the first foreigner to lead the institution.

In this role, he would face the economic turmoil caused by Brexit, after the UK decided to leave the European Union.

Declaring Monday that "America has changed," the Canadian leader is moving forward with determination: seeking new trading partners, launching major projects and boosting military spending.

Carney has notably forged closer ties with the EU and is set to discuss soon the strengthening of that partnership.

In Armenia in May, he emphasized that the EU and Canada were not "doomed" to submit to a "brutal" international order.

Carney was born in Fort Smith, a remote town in Canada's Northwest Territories, and was raised in Edmonton, Alberta, a province rich in hydrocarbons.

He wants to construct a new pipeline to the Pacific in order to export Canadian oil to Asia and thus reduce the need to sell to the American market.

But by "putting his foot down" with Trump, Frederic Boily, a political science professor at the University of Alberta, Carney "will now enter a somewhat more difficult phase" where he will have to manage the impact on Canada's economy and his popularity.

articles.title: Paxton unveils data center plan
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Paxton unveils data center plan Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) unveiled a plan for data centers if elected to the U.S. Senate, becoming the latest GOP candidate to take a stronger stance against the controversial AI infrastructure. © Tony Gutierrez, Associated Press Paxton laid out…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) unveiled a plan for data centers if elected to the U.S. Senate, becoming the latest GOP candidate to take a stronger stance against the controversial AI infrastructure.

Paxton laid out his four-point plan, vowing to “fiercely advocate” for Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R) state-level data center plan and sponsor or back various federal legislation.

This includes legislation that would bar the use of Chinese technology to power data centers.

He also said he would co-sponsor the Decentralized Access to Technology Alternatives Act, a bill from Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) that would exempt new, off-grid electricity providers from certain federal regulations in an effort to prevent data centers from raising consumer electricity costs.

“My Texas First Data Center Plan will protect our grid, our communities, and our children while ensuring America beats Communist China in the AI race,” Paxton wrote in a post on the social platform X.

articles.title: As Trump pulls back school civil rights enforcement, who will protect Black students?
articles.summary: Education policy experts say states and school districts must step up as federal officials retreat from using racial disparities to
articles.body:
Education policy experts say states and school districts must step up as federal officials retreat from using racial disparities to investigate discrimination.

After the Trump administration moved to eliminate guidance on considering race in school discipline , education experts are sounding the alarm about how the Education Department's new rule will impact Black students at a time when they are facing existing setbacks in the classroom.

As theGrio previously reported, the Trump administration recently reversed a 2014 guidance issued by the Obama administration that encouraged schools to examine student discipline data for racial disparities, as Black students were suspended at disproportionately high rates.

The Trump administration now argues that the guidance is discriminatory against white students, or is, in other words, resulting in reverse discrimination. But Eric Duncan, director of P-12 policy at EdTrust, tells theGrio, the data doesn't support that argument.

"If you look at some of the previous civil rights reports, you'll see cases where schools or districts will…treat Black students differently for the same offenses as white students," said Duncan. "They'll suspend them or expel them, whereas for white students, they'll call conferences."

The guidance issued by Kimberly Richey, the Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights at the Education Department, claims the Obama-era guidance on school discipline, known as disparate impact liability, led to "increased violence and other disruptions at school."

Phelton Moss, Ph.D., an assistant professor at Virginia Commonwealth University and an expert on anti-racist practices in K–12 Schools, tells theGrio that there is no evidence of a "throughline" showing that considering disproportionate disciplinary outcomes for Black students results in violent or greater disruption in the classroom.

"What is true since the Obama administration is that we have been able to find instances where there are gaps in terms of access to opportunity, and we've been able to address those gaps to access to opportunity because of these data," Moss told theGrio.

Now, educational experts are left questioning: who will protect Black students?

The new guidance from the Trump administration comes at a fragile time for Black students across the country, as data shows racial gaps in literacy and math outcomes for Black students , particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in students having to learn through computer screens at home.

Duncan emphasizes that, regardless of the new Trump administration guidance, the legal disparate impact framework, created in 1964 through the Civil Rights Act, remains on the books. However, its application has varied through court rulings over the years, and the Trump administration has essentially abandoned racial discrimination investigations in schools. The Education Department gutted its Office of Civil Rights and eliminated some of its regional offices.

"What has happened is a lot of these claims, based on these types of racial issues are being largely ignored," Duncan told theGrio.

Still, experts tell theGrio that states and Congress can still step in to ensure that Black students do not fall victim to the discrimination in school disciplinary action of years past.

"States can create their own civil rights protections under state law and enforce disparate impact at the school level, and provide support, remedies, resources, whatever, for their schools when issues arise, and there are violations of the law," said Duncan.

Duncan noted that in December 2025, New Jersey passed a law codifying and reinforcing the principle that neutral business policies that harm protected groups violate the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination, even without discriminatory intent.

Moss agrees, telling theGrio, "If this administration is hell-bent on returning education to the states, which they are actively and progressively doing each day, then the states must step up and ensure and codify these protections."

He continued, "I do think states that care about data and states that care about kids who have grown up on the margins of society being in a safe learning environment will take this to task and will codify it in their existing state laws."

But Moss is calling for one step further.

"Congress has the ability to provide carrots or sticks so they can beat this administration into doing this, or they can incentivize this administration to do it by making it a condition of their budget, if Congress has the will to do that," he explained.

Without intervention from states or Congress, Black students and their families are left to prove intentional discrimination, which Moss notes is a "very high evidence bar," whereas before they were able to "rely" on data that if you suspend 40% of Black children, "you've put them on the school-to-prison pipeline."

He added, "Now we can't rely on that to determine that there's a culture of discrimination inside a school system or a school building."

articles.body:
Democrats are ahead 7 points on the economy over Republicans, according to a new poll.

In The Economist/YouGov poll , 39 percent of respondents said they believe Democrats do “a better job handling” the economy, while 32 said the same of Republicans. Fifteen percent said both parties handle the economy “about the same” and another 15 percent were unsure.

As the midterms near, a number of Democrats have made affordability a key plank of their campaigns, especially amid the Iran war’s effects on the cost of living and wider concerns about the economy.

Since the start of the war in Iran, oil and gas prices have risen as the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the global oil industry, has been closed. According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of regular gas Tuesday evening was about $4.10, up from about $3.16 last year .

Last week, the Trump administration ended summertime smog limits on gasoline earlier than usual in an attempt to offer relief for high gas costs. articles.title: 2 people die from measles in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story Two people die from measles in Pennsylvania Two unvaccinated people died from the measles in Pennsylvania, marking the first deaths the state has seen in 35 years and the first in the country this year. © AP Photo/Annie Rice, File…
articles.body:
Two people die from measles in Pennsylvania

Two unvaccinated people died from the measles in Pennsylvania, marking the first deaths the state has seen in 35 years and the first in the country this year.

Both people were residents of Lancaster County, the heart of the state’s Amish population, but officials did not disclose any additional information. Pennsylvania has confirmed 393 measles cases in 28 counties this year, including 86 in the past week.

Across the country, five people have died from measles in the past two years, more than the past 30 years combined .

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) said he confronted Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. about the federal government’s role in spreading misinformation that he said is contributing to declining vaccination rates.

“I was very, very blunt with him, and I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said.

“There’s real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors and actual medical professionals to provide unbiased information to parents so that we can make reasonable decisions for our kids,” he added.

The measles surge has hit at the same time as the Trump administration is taking steps to reduce and space out the number of childhood vaccinations, including an executive order to split up the combination measles, mumps and rubella vaccine— something pediatricians say is dangerous and that would result in fewer vaccinations.

President Trump falsely said the combined MMR shot was “lethal,” and both Trump and Kennedy have falsely insinuated t hat an increase in the number of childhood vaccines is linked to a rise in autism rates.

Kennedy has acknowledged that “the most effective way to prevent the spread of measles is the MMR vaccine” but has also falsely said it has not been safety tested, and that it offers only short-term protection that wanes quickly.

In a contentious CNN interview earlier this month, Kennedy said he takes no responsibility for the country’s measles outbreaks and blamed COVID-19 “lockdowns” for declining vaccination rates.

The New York Times reported that Kennedy spoke in Lancaster County five years ago when he was the leader of Children’s Health Defense, one of the country’s most prominent anti-vaccine groups .

Kennedy reportedly downplayed the severity of measles infections and warned members of the Amish community that public health agencies will force them to vaccinate.

articles.title: Gavin Newsom puts Spanish-style California mansion up for sale for $7.5m
articles.summary: The 12-bath, seven-bed home near the state capital boasts a 5,000-bottle wine cellar, a pool and a tennis court
articles.body:
California governor Gavin Newsom has put his Sacramento-area mansion up for sale, before his term will end in January.

The 12-bath, seven-bed Spanish-style home in Fair Oaks, a suburb of the California capital, hit the market on Monday with an asking price of $7.5m. The estate, which sits on a 8.2-acre (3.3-hectare) parcel of land, boasts an array of amenities including a full-size tennis court, a 5,000-bottle wine cellar, a pool, a cold plunge and a hot tub, according to a Zillow listing from realtors Matthew Hindy and Nick Sadek.

Newsom, who was elected California governor in 2018, is openly considering running for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.

The governor and his family moved into the Fair Oaks property in 2019, after briefly living at the historic governor's mansion in Sacramento. A spokesperson, at the time, described the estate as "more kid-friendly", according to the Sacramento Bee.

The Newsoms have since split their time between Sacramento and Marin county, an affluent area north of San Francisco, where they also own property. Newsom enrolled his children in Marin county schools in 2024.

The Fair Oaks mansion was the site of a protest in 2020, where protesters chained themselves to its fence to denounce rising California prison deaths amid the coronavirus pandemic.

The property also received attention when Newsom used it to host a 2024 political fundraiser for Minnesota governor Tim Walz, who was then campaigning as the Democratic vice-presidential candidate.

articles.title: Trump’s pick for open House seat in Kentucky scrubs president from campaign website
articles.summary: President Trump’s pick to replace Republican Rep. Andy Barr (Ky.) in the House has completely scrubbed the president from his campaign website. Former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado’s (R) campaign website no longer features an image of the candidate next to Trump with them both giving a thumbs-up and shifted from branding himself as a national…
articles.body:
President Trump’s pick to replace Republican Rep. Andy Barr (Ky.) in the House has completely scrubbed the president from his campaign website.

Former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado’s (R) campaign website no longer features an image of the candidate next to Trump with them both giving a thumbs-up and shifted from branding himself as a national leader in the “America First” movement to an “independent” focused on healthcare.

The scrub of his website was first reported by NBC .

Alvarado and the White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment explaining the change.

An archived version of Alvarado’s website says he “was one of President Trump’s earliest supporters, and now he’s stepping up to fight alongside him in Washington to fire up the economy, secure our border, and stop the woke agenda.”

It touted the former state senator as the only Latino to speak in support of Trump at the 2016 Republican National Convention.

Now statements on the website focus on healthcare and lowering costs.

“Healthcare isn’t a talking point to me — it’s been my life’s work. In Congress, I’ll work with both parties to fight for affordable healthcare, lower costs, and practical solutions that help Kentucky families,” a quote from Alvarado on the campaign website’s landing page says.

His statement comes as healthcare premiums increased after lawmakers decided not to renew Affordable Care Act subsidies and as the Trump administration pushes changes to the vaccine schedule for school-age children.

Democrats say Alvarado’s shift in rhetoric shows that he’s “two-faced.”

“He is a two-faced, corrupt politician who has shown he is willing to say anything to deceive Central Kentuckians just to try and get elected,” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson Eli Cousin told The Hill.

“Alvarado scrubbing his website to try and paper over his real record is just the latest sign that he is feeling the heat and knows that this race is a true toss up,” Cousin added.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the seat vacated by Barr as “ likely Republican .”

articles.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom puts Sacramento-area mansion up for sale
articles.summary: As California Gov. Gavin Newsom is set to leave office at the end of this term, he has placed his Sacramento-area mansion on the market.
articles.body:
As California Gov. Gavin Newsom is set to leave the state's highest office at the end of this term, he and his partner, Jennifer Newsom, have placed their Sacramento-based mansion on the market.

The 12,663 sq ft mansion is located in Sacramento County's unincorporated area at 7640 Tobia Way in Fair Oaks , about 25 minutes from downtown Sacramento, and was listed for sale by Sotheby's International Realty for a whopping $7.5 million.

See inside Gavin Newsom's Sacramento-area mansion on sale for $7.5M

The property is "an extraordinary showcase of Santa Barbara-inspired architecture," hidden behind a private gate and "exceptionally secluded."

"This remarkable Fair Oaks estate is privately positioned along the bluffs on 8.2 acres, where sweeping views and exceptional privacy create a truly rare setting," reads the listing description.

"Spanning approximately 12,663 square feet, the residence offers an unparalleled combination of grandeur, comfort, and effortless entertaining, with a resort-style pool, full-size tennis court, private casita, and impressive 5,000-bottle wine cellar. The expansive primary bathroom is a destination unto itself, designed as a serene retreat with two generous walk-in closets, dual showers and water closets, and a luxurious soaking tub."

Matthew Hindy, the listing agent with Nick Sadek Sotheby's International Realty , noted that the mansion was "a beautiful property" and that it "holds a special charm."

The Newsoms purchased the property in December 2018 for nearly half the price, at $3.7 million, shortly before he assumed the Governor's Office. Newsom and his family did briefly live in California's governor's mansion, which was renovated for former Governor Jerry Brown, before ultimately relocating to the Fair Oaks property.

However, the sale of Newsom's Fair Oaks property may not come as a surprise to anyone who follows the governor closely, as in 2024, the Newsoms purchased a $9.1 million home in the unincorporated community of Kentfield.

As Newsom's tenure as California's governor drew closer to its end, he spent less time in Sacramento, splitting his time between the Capitol and the San Francisco Bay Area.

Ultimately, the sale of this property marks the end of Newsom's time in the Sacramento area and leaves an opportunity for him to prepare for a potential 2028 presidential bid, as he is seen as a likely frontrunner in the upcoming election .

Noe Padilla is a Northern California Reporter for USA Today. Contact him at npadilla@usatodayco.com, follow him on X @1NoePadilla or on Bluesky @noepadilla.bsky.social. Sign up for the TODAY Californian newsletter or follow us on Facebook at TODAY Californian .

articles.title: RNC Send Bizarre Fundraising Text Purporting To Be From JD Vance: ‘Groceries Cost What They Cost’
articles.summary: The Republican National Committee reportedly sent a fundraising text in Vice President JD Vance’s name on Tuesday, bluntly declaring, “Groceries cost what th...
articles.body:
The Republican National Committee reportedly sent a fundraising text in Vice President JD Vance's name on Tuesday, bluntly declaring, "Groceries cost what they cost."

The message was shared on X by The Washington Post's Natalie Allison , who covers the White House and President Donald Trump's MAGA movement for the paper. Her screenshot of the call to donate read, "If you can't give right now, don't, Natalie. Groceries cost what they cost."

While there is an online archive of political emails , no such database exists for text messages, meaning Mediaite has only seen the above message through Allison's X post. However, after the wild groceries jab, the text continued, "But can you answer this for me," alongside a link. Using the copy-and-paste feature from the screenshot, Mediaite has independently verified that the link in question takes users to a webpage titled "A letter from JD Vance."

The lengthy statement largely centered on distrust of political fundraising, with Vance — or whoever authored the message in his name — apologizing for tactics like "countdown clocks that expire at midnight and reset by morning."

"I'll tell you the truth, including the parts you don't want to hear," the letter pledged, before eventually acknowledging, "The Republican National Committee needs money."

The page then repeated the line from the text message: "If you can't give right now, don't. Groceries cost what they cost. I'm not going to make you feel guilty over a number."

But the fundraising page itself struck a somewhat different tone. Visitors were presented with several suggested donation amounts, including a preselected $47 contribution. The page also featured an option to donate recurringly and another checkbox asking donors to contribute an additional $47 on Aug. 28 while declaring, "ILLEGALS ARE TAKING YOUR MEDICAID BENEFITS!"

Another checkbox read, "VERIFY: I told JD Vance the truth."

Notably, the message comes just days after Vance spoke on affordability in his hometown of Middletown, Ohio, where he claimed the Trump administration was making the "American dream of homeownership" accessible to young people again and incorrectly asserted that rents were falling "for the first time in over five years."

The post RNC Send Bizarre Fundraising Text Purporting To Be From JD Vance: 'Groceries Cost What They Cost' first appeared on Mediaite .

articles.title: 'Unconscionable': Lawyers hit back after DOJ suggests Kennedy Center demolition
articles.summary: A DOJ court filing argues the center faces a "death spiral" without Trump help.
articles.body:
The Justice Department suggested in a court filing Tuesday that the Kennedy Center could face demolition in the event a federal judge issues an order permanently blocking President Donald Trump's push to renovate the facility with additions intended to recognize Trump personally.

In an extraordinary filing that at times reads like a post from Trump's social media platform, Brantley Mayers — a top official in DOJ's Civil Division — argues the "decrepit" Kennedy Center faces an imminent "death spiral" without Trump's intervention.

"Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years," the filing said. "Such a replacement will fail to adequately honor President John F. Kennedy, but would be simpler and more economical to build, operate, and maintain."

Mayers uses the filing to repeatedly attack Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, a member of the Kennedy Center's board who filed suit last year to have Trump's name removed from the building. Beatty's lawsuit argued the board's vote to rename the building was illegal because an act of Congress is required for such an action.

Permitting Beatty's legal efforts to continue, Mayers warns the federal judge overseeing the lawsuit, "almost guarantees the continued decline and eventual demise of the Kennedy Center, probably leading to the construction of a new, but very different kind, of venue."

Kennedy Center board votes to close for renovations and add Trump's name again, lawmaker says

In a statement responding to the papers filed by the Department of Justice on Tuesday, lawyers for Beatty called DOJ's filing "legally baseless" and said it was "unconscionable" that DOJ would threaten to demolish the Kennedy Center if the court were to block the planned renovations.

"This is a not-so-subtle threat to demolish the Kennedy Center if the President doesn't get his way. This is unconscionable, it is unbecoming of the Department of Justice to even put this in a filing, and we will answer in court," attorneys Norman Eisen Nathaniel Zelinsky said in a statement.

The DOJ describes the initiatives approved by the Kennedy Center's board that intend to honor Trump personally for his effort — including adding the inscription "Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump" on the front of the building and renaming the site that contains the Center the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza" — as "crucial" to ensure payments from donors who have already pledged to help fund the renovation effort.

"An order blocking the Board from appropriately recognizing President Trump will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop," the department argues. "There will simply not be the expertise or funding necessary to rebuild and renovate this decimated structure. The Trump Administration is ready to go but, without it, the Kennedy Center cannot be saved."

U.S. District Judge Christopher Coper has scheduled a hearing for 2 p.m. Thursday on an emergency motion filed by Beatty seeking an injunction to block the re-adding of Trump's name on the performing arts center.

articles.title: Hegseth, Loeffler announce commission to surge aid to small defense contractors
articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & NatSec newsletter {beacon} Defense &National Security Defense &National Security The Big Story Hegseth, Loeffler announce commission to surge aid to small defense contractors Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Small Business Administration (SBA) Administrator Kelly Loeffler announced on Tuesday the establishment of a Smaller War Plants Commission that would…
articles.body:
Hegseth, Loeffler announce commission to surge aid to small defense contractors

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Small Business Administration (SBA) Administrator Kelly Loeffler announced on Tuesday the establishment of a Smaller War Plants Commission that would surge expertise and funds to smaller defense companies.

“Our message is clear: President Trump is ending the era of dependence on foreign supply chains and our adversaries. This historic long-term commitment will reinforce the industrial depth that stands proudly behind the strongest military on earth. When we back the businesses who supply our forces, we outbuild, out innovate and overwhelm any adversary,” Hegseth said in a 3-minute video posted on social platform X. “We are transforming industrial capability into generational battlefield advantage, and in doing so, we will deter conflict , preserve peace and ensure that no adversary tests American strength,” Hegseth said. The new commission was billed as an equivalent to the Smaller War Plants Corporation , which was formed by Congress in 1942 to aid small businesses in building war supplies during World War II. It made loans, obtained contracts and provided technical assistance to small plants. “Our joint mission will supercharge funding to those building our supply chain, tooling up, expanding, innovating and hiring to deliver capability to the warfighter,” Loeffler said in the same video. “The era of offshoring the production of power projection to our adversaries is over.” Small manufacturers comprise 70 percent of the U.S. defense industrial base , according to Loeffler, who added that SBA oversees nearly $500 billion in small business portfolio. “Thanks to President Trump and Secretary Hegseth, the world’s strongest military will be backed by the world’s most nimble industrial base , offering our warfighters asymmetric advantage and our nation peace through strength,” the SBA administrator said.

articles.title: Titanic artifacts auction blocked by federal judge
articles.summary: A federal judge in Virginia blocked an auction of more than 100 century-old artifacts that were salvaged from the shipwrecked RMS Titanic vessel, calling their selling “an apparent threat” to the collection’s integrity and preservation. U.S. District Judge Rebecca Beach Smith ordered RMS Titanic — the company with exclusive salvage rights to the wreckage —…
articles.body:
A federal judge in Virginia blocked an auction of more than 100 century-old artifacts that were salvaged from the shipwrecked RMS Titanic vessel, calling their selling “an apparent threat” to the collection’s integrity and preservation.

U.S. District Judge Rebecca Beach Smith ordered RMS Titanic — the company with exclusive salvage rights to the wreckage — to pause its auction after the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the French government opposed the sale.

Smith said in her decision that any sale of items related to the Titanic would be subject to the court’s approval, The Washington Post reported Tuesday.

RMS Titanic first struck the deal for salvaging rights in 2011, though the auction puts the arrangement in a complicated situation.

The company wanted to auction the items earlier this year after making salvage claims in a U.S. District Court in Norfolk, Virginia, arguing they were facing “financial difficulties,” according to The New York Times .

The judge pushed back on this claim due to the fact that RMS Titanic’s partial owner — private equity firm Apollo Global Management — reportedly earns “billions of dollars in annual revenue and assets under management.”

NOAA argued the auction would separate the collection that already has competing claims. The agency’s website adds that RMS Titanic entered an agreement with a French court related to the artifacts stipulating that they must be “managed together … as a whole intact collection.”

The ship crashed on April 15, 1912 — killing roughly 1,500 of its 2,200 passengers. The wreck has since become a source of public fascination.

In 2023, for example, five people died when OceanGate’s submersible imploded while trying to visit the wreckage — located hundreds of miles below sea in the North Atlantic.

In April, a life jacket worn by a passenger of the crash that was signed by survivors sold for more than $900,000.

“These record-breaking prices illustrate the continuing interest in the Titanic story, and the respect for the passengers and crew whose stories are immortalized by these items of memorabilia,” auctioneer Andrew Aldridge said about the sale.

RMS Titanic did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment on the court’s decision.

articles.title: Trump threatens to demolish Kennedy Center if $250m renovation not done
articles.summary: US president’s lawyers in court filing say Washington arts complex must undergo repairs or risk demolition
articles.body:
The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts could be demolished if repairs are not carried out, the Trump administration warned in a court filing on Monday.

Lawyers for the US president said the national arts complex in Washington DC must undergo a $250m renovation or risk facing the wrecking ball.

"Without those efforts, the ⁠Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to ​build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years," they argued.

The warning came as Donald Trump leaves a trail of destruction in Washington, demolishing the East Wing of the White House to make way for a $600m ballroom and ordering a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool that resulted in algae blooms and a peeling liner.

Related: Father of USS Lincoln sailor detained by ICE released from detention

The court filing represented the first time that Trump's allies have raised the prospect of knocking down the Kennedy Center – a 100ft-high complex with a concert hall, opera house and theatre – as the dire alternative to closing it for two years of improvements. Such an aggressive move would be sure to face legal challenges, protests and an outcry from historic preservation groups.

The threat emerged on Monday as the administration urged a federal judge to reject a fresh legal challenge to Trump's efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center. The dispute has become part of a months-long battle over the president's attempt to alter the memorial created by Congress in honour of John F Kennedy , the 35th US president, who was assassinated in 1963.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

A federal judge ruled in May that only Congress has the power to change the Kennedy Center's name. But the centre's board, now largely made up of Trump appointees, voted 20-3 on 13 August to change the building's signage to read "The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump". It also voted to name the grounds the "President Donald J Trump Plaza".

The administration argued the latest proposal did not breach the court's injunction because the building would still formally be called the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The words "Restored and Renovated by" merely acknowledge Trump's role, lawyers said, comparing the inscription to acknowledgments of major donors at other cultural institutions.

The filing was made in response to a request by Joyce Beatty , a Democratic congresswoman from Ohio and a member of the Kennedy Center board by virtue of her position in Congress, to stop Trump's name being restored to the facade.

Beatty sued last year after the centre altered its white marble facade to read "The Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts". In May, Judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump's name removed, ruling that the venue "must be named for, and is meant to honor, President Kennedy alone".

Cooper added: "Congress named the Kennedy Center and only Congress can change it."

Trump's name was removed from the facade in June and a big tarpaulin has covered the affected section of the building since then. An appeals court last month rejected the administration's request to keep the name in place while it challenges Cooper's ruling.

Nathaniel Zelinsky, a lawyer for Beatty, described Monday's filing as legally baseless and said it "reads like it was written personally by Donald Trump". Judge Cooper is due to hear Beatty's request for an injunction at a hearing in federal court in Washington on Thursday.

The Kennedy Center was established by Congress as a living memorial to Kennedy and opened in 1971. It has hosted stars ranging from Frank Sinatra and Beyoncé to Robert De Niro and Lin-Manuel Miranda. It has been limping artistically and commercially since Trump took over last year, culling staff and declaring war on "woke" programming.

On Tuesday, the Washington Post reported that ticket sales, already down since Trump seized control, plummeted further after his board of trustees voted in December to rename the complex after him and put his name on its marble facade.

Norm Eisen , a former White House "ethics czar" and co-founder of the nonpartisan group Democracy Defenders Action , posted on social media that "the administration is now threatening in federal court to LEVEL the Kennedy Center if Trump does not get his way. His path of destruction knows no bounds & he will answer for it in court."

John Larson, a Democratic congressman from Connecticut, condemned Trump's threat. "No one is surprised that someone with an ego as big as Donald Trump's believes their name should be above John F Kennedy's on our beloved former president's living memorial," said Larson. "I wish President Trump were more focused on ending the illegal war he launched in Iran than he is on destroying the Kennedy Center and building his taxpayer-funded ballroom."

Hands Off the Arts, a group of more than 2,800 activists opposed to government censorship of the arts, said in a statement: "President Trump today issued the judge and American people a threat: 'Allow me to hijack JFK's memorial or I will turn it into a crater.' As Americans, we have already watched in anger the obliteration of the East Wing to satisfy Trump's vanity – we won't let it happen again to the Kennedy Center. This is the people's memorial to honor JFK, and we refuse to let it be desecrated or demolished."

articles.title: Bolivia's Paz taps deputy to lead economy after minister's ousting
articles.summary: LA PAZ, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz appointed Christian Morales as economy and public finance minister on Tuesday, signaling policy con...
articles.body:
LA PAZ, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz appointed Christian Morales as economy and public finance minister ‌on Tuesday, signaling policy continuity as his government ‌seeks to stabilize the crisis-hit economy, secure foreign financing and push reforms through ​Congress.

Morales, who served as deputy minister under Jose Gabriel Espinoza, takes over after lawmakers last week censured and removed Espinoza in a blow to Paz.

The leadership change comes at a delicate ‌moment for Bolivia, which ⁠is grappling with falling natural gas output, low foreign-currency reserves, fuel shortages and a shortage of ⁠U.S. dollars.
